~~~text
\begin{multline}\label{eq:defspaceintwod}
\boldsymbol{V}_{\od\cap\boldsymbol{\delta}}^{\rm m, +\od}\Lambda^k=\boldsymbol{V}_{{\rm rot}\cap{\rm div}}^{\rm m, +{\rm rot}}:=\Bigg\{\boldsymbol{\mu}_h\in\prod_{T\inP}^{*,-}_1\Lambda{\mathbf{P}_{\odelta}^{\rm m}\Lambda{G}_h}\mathbf{P}^{\rm m+rot}_{{\rm rot}\cap{\rm div}}(T):
({\rm rot}_h\boldsymbol{\mu}_h,\boldsymbol{\eta}_h)-(\boldsymbol{\mu}_h,{\rm curl}\boldsymbol{\eta}_h)=0,\ \forall\,\boldsymbol{\eta}_h\in V^1_{h0},
\\
\mbox{and}\ \ ({\rm div}_h\boldsymbol{\mu}_h,\boldsymbol{\tau}_h)-(\boldsymbol{\mu}_h,{\rm grad}\boldsymbol{\tau}_h)=0,\forall\,\boldsymbol{\tau}_h\in V^1_h. \Bigg\}
\end{multline}

Now we present the basis functions of $\boldsymbol{V}_{\od\cap\boldsymbol{\delta}}^{\rm m, +\od}\Lambda^k$ by a 3-step procedure. 

\paragraph{\bf Step 1} Both $V^1_h$ and $V^1_{h0}$ admit locally supported basis functions, denoted by $\phi_a$ and $\psi_a$ associated with vertices $a\inP}^{*,-}_1\Lambda{\mathbf{P}_{\odelta}^{\rm m}\Lambda{X}_h$ and $a\inP}^{*,-}_1\Lambda{\mathbf{P}_{\odelta}^{\rm m}\Lambda{X}_h^i$, respectively. The restrictions of $\phi_a$ and $\psi_a$ on a triangle are each one of the barycentric coordinates on the triangle. We refer to Figure \ref{fig:vertices} for an illustration of interior and boundary vertices, and also the supports of $\phi_a$($\psi_a$). 

\paragraph{\bf Step 2} On a cell $T$, with $a_i\inP}^{*,-}_1\Lambda{\mathbf{P}_{\odelta}^{\rm m}\Lambda{X}_h$ being its vertices, let $\lambda^{a_i}_T$ be the barycentric coordinates of $T$, and find $\boldsymbol{\mu}^{{\rm div}}_{a_i,T},\ \boldsymbol{\mu}^{{\rm rot}}_{a_i,T}\in \mathbf{P}_{\od\cap\odelta}^{\rm m+\od}\Lambda^1(T)$, $1\leqslant i\leqslant 3$, such that 
$$
({\rm rot} \boldsymbol{\mu}^{{\rm div}}_{a_i,T},\lambda_T^{a_j})_T-(\boldsymbol{\mu}^{{\rm div}}_{a_i,T},{\rm curl}\lambda_T^{a_j})=0,\ \  ({\rm div}\boldsymbol{\mu}^{{\rm div}}_{a_i,T},\lambda_T^{a_j})_T-(\boldsymbol{\mu}^{{\rm div}}_{a_i,T},{\rm grad}\lambda_T^{a_j})=\delta_{ij}, \ \ 1\leqslant i,j\leqslant 3,
$$
and
$$
({\rm rot} \boldsymbol{\mu}^{{\rm rot}}_{a_i,T},\lambda_T^{a_j})_T-(\boldsymbol{\mu}^{{\rm div}}_{a_i,T},{\rm curl}\lambda_T^{a_j})=\delta_{ij},\ \  ({\rm div}\boldsymbol{\mu}^{{\rm rot}}_{a_i,T},\lambda_T^{a_j})_T-(\boldsymbol{\mu}^{{\rm div}}_{a_i,T},{\rm grad}\lambda_T^{a_j})=0,\ \ 1\leqslant i,j\leqslant 3. 
$$

\paragraph{\bf Step 3} The global basis functions of $\boldsymbol{V}_{\od\cap\boldsymbol{\delta}}^{\rm m, +\od}\Lambda^k$ fall into two categories, corresponding to $\boldsymbol{V}_{\boldsymbol{\delta}}$ ($\boldsymbol{V}_{{\rm div}}$ here) and $\boldsymbol{V}_{\od}$ ($\boldsymbol{V}_{{\rm rot}}$ here), respectively. 
\begin{description}
\item[Category I] All these functions in ${\rm span}\{\boldsymbol{\mu}^{{\rm div}}_{a,T}:a\inP}^{*,-}_1\Lambda{\mathbf{P}_{\odelta}^{\rm m}\Lambda{X}_h,\ T\inP}^{*,-}_1\Lambda{\mathbf{P}_{\odelta}^{\rm m}\Lambda{G}_h\}$ such that conditions in \eqref{eq:defspaceintwod} are satisfied with respect to every $\phi_a\in V^1_h$ a basis function. Particularly, with respect to any vertex $a$, the associated basis functions of $\boldsymbol{V}_{\od\cap\boldsymbol{\delta}}^{\rm m, +\od}\Lambda^k$ are all these functions in ${\rm span}\{\boldsymbol{\mu}^{{\rm div}}_{a,T}:\mathring{T}\cap {\rm supp}(\phi_a)\neq\emptyset\}$, namely, functions 
$$
\boldsymbol{\omega}_h=\sum_{\partial T\ni a}c_TE_T^\Omega\boldsymbol{\mu}^{{\rm div}}_{a,T},\ \ \mbox{such\ that}\ 
\sum_{\partial T\ni a}({\rm div}\boldsymbol{\omega}_h,\phi_a|_T)_T+(\boldsymbol{\omega}_h,\nabla\phi_a|_T)_T=0.
$$
Those $\boldsymbol{\omega}_h$ in this category are each supported in a two-successive-cell patch. We refer to Figure \ref{fig:basisinteriorvertex} for the case $a\inP}^{*,-}_1\Lambda{\mathbf{P}_{\odelta}^{\rm m}\Lambda{X}_h^i$, and to Figure \ref{fig:boundaryvertex} (right) for an illustration that $a\inP}^{*,-}_1\Lambda{\mathbf{P}_{\odelta}^{\rm m}\Lambda{X}_h^b$. 

\item[Category II] All these functions in ${\rm span}\{\boldsymbol{\mu}^{{\rm rot}}_{a,T}:a\inP}^{*,-}_1\Lambda{\mathbf{P}_{\odelta}^{\rm m}\Lambda{X}_h,\ T\inP}^{*,-}_1\Lambda{\mathbf{P}_{\odelta}^{\rm m}\Lambda{G}_h\}$ such that conditions in \eqref{eq:defspaceintwod} are satisfied with respect to every $\psi_a\in V^1_{h0}$ a basis function. Particularly, with respect to an interior vertex $a$, the associated basis functions of $\boldsymbol{V}_{\od\cap\boldsymbol{\delta}}^{\rm m, +\od}\Lambda^k$ are all these functions in ${\rm span}\{\boldsymbol{\mu}^{{\rm rot}}_{a,T}:\mathring{T}\cap {\rm supp}(\phi_a)\neq\emptyset\}$, namely, functions 
$$
\boldsymbol{\omega}_h=\sum_{\partial T\ni a}c_TE_T^\Omega\boldsymbol{\mu}^{{\rm rot}}_{a,T},\ \mbox{such\ that}\ \sum_{\partial T\ni a}({\rm rot}\boldsymbol{\omega}_h,\phi_a|_T)_T-(\boldsymbol{\omega}_h,{\rm curl}\phi_a|_T)_T=0.
$$
Those $\boldsymbol{\omega}_h$ in this category are each supported in a two-successive-cell patch. We refer to Figure \ref{fig:basisinteriorvertex} for the case $a\inP}^{*,-}_1\Lambda{\mathbf{P}_{\odelta}^{\rm m}\Lambda{X}_h^i$. 

With respect to a boundary vertex $a$, the associated basis functions of $\boldsymbol{V}_{\od\cap\boldsymbol{\delta}}^{\rm m, +\od}\Lambda^k$ are all these functions in ${\rm span}\{\boldsymbol{\mu}^{{\rm rot}}_{a,T}:\mathring{T}\cap {\rm supp}(\phi_a)\neq\emptyset\}$. The supports of the functions are each a single triangle. We refer to Figure \ref{fig:boundaryvertex}, left, for an illustration. 
\end{description}
~~~

## Q11-0012

~~~text
\section{Introduction}\label{SIntro}

We construct a process that mimics certain
properties of a given It\^o process, but is
simpler in the sense that the mimicking process
solves a stochastic differential equation (SDE),
while the It\^o process may have drift and
diffusion terms that are themselves stochastic processes.
This work is motivated by the problem of model
calibration in finance.  The financial engineer
would like to identify a class of models for
an underlying asset price that are
flexible enough to allow for calibration to a wide
range of possible market prices of derivative securities
on that asset.  The result of this paper shows the extent to which
sophisticated models are no more powerful
for calibration purposes than an SDE
for the underlying asset price.

Our results are closely related to Krylov \cite{Kry3} and
Gy\"ongy \cite{G}.  Krylov \cite{Kry3} calls the measure that
records the average amount of time that
an It\^o process $X$ spends in each Borel set
before being killed at the first jump of an
independent Poisson
process with intensity $\lambda$ the
{\em Green $\lambda$-measure} of $X$.
Given an It\^o process with
bounded drift and bounded, uniformly
positive-definite covariance,
Krylov \cite{Kry3} constructs a
process with the same Green $\lambda$-measure
which solves a
time-independent diffusion equation.  Krylov
further asserts that it
is possible to construct a process that solves
a time-dependent
diffusion equation and matches the
one-dimensional marginal
distributions of such an It\^o process.
Gy\"ongy \cite{G} provides a
proof of Krylov's assertion and shows that
the drift and
\gbmarginpar{Removed the word ``coefficients'' because the covariance isn't
  the coefficient in the SDE and we really mean the SDE not the
  PDE here.  I'm not sure this a really an improvement, so feel free
  to add it back.  It doesn't change the page breaks.
covariance in the diffusion
equation solved by the
mimicking process may be interpreted as the expected value of the
It\^o process's instantaneous drift and covariance conditioned on its
level.
See also Klebaner \cite{Kleb} for a
related argument
based on semimartingale local time.

Gy\"ongy \cite{G} was rediscovered by the mathematical finance
community in the context of local volatility models.
Dupire \cite{Dup1} studies the European option prices generated by
a model in which the risk-neutral dynamics of the price process
satisfy a time-dependent diffusion equation
(see also Derman and Kani \cite{DK1} for a discrete-time treatment
of this topic). These models are now
known as {\em local volatility models}, and the diffusion coefficient of the
log-price process is known as the {\em local volatility surface}.
Dupire \cite{Dup1} shows that it is possible to construct a local
volatility model that
is consistent with a given set of European option prices when that set
of prices is sufficiently smooth as a function of maturity and strike,
and he shows how the local volatility surface may be implied directly
from the call prices.  Local volatility models have proven popular
with practitioners because they allow for calibration to a wide range
of European option prices.  Dupire \cite{Dup1} does not find the
dynamics of a local volatility model to be particularly plausible;
however, he asserts that ``the market prices European options
\textit{as if} the process was this diffusion.''  In effect, the local
volatility model mimics the European option prices of some more
complicated market process, and this is equivalent to matching the
one-dimensional marginal distributions of
that process under the equivalent martingale
probability measure (also call the
{\em risk-neutral measure}) used for pricing.

In \cite{Dup2}, Dupire extends \cite{Dup1} to
study the local volatility surface that is implied
not by market prices of options but by prices
generated from a stochastic volatility model.  Using
infinitesimal calendar and butterfly spreads, he
presents a financial argument that the square of
the local volatility function is the expected value
of the instantaneous squared stochastic volatility
conditioned on the level of the underlying asset
price, essentially recovering Gy\"ongy's result,
albeit in a nonrigorous fashion.  Following this
development, the Gy\"ongy-Dupire formula has found
several applications in finance.  For example,
Gatheral \cite{Gat} uses it to compare the
properties of a number of stochastic volatility
models, and Antonov and Misirpashaev \cite{AM}
and Piterbarg \cite{Pit2,Pit4,Pit5} combine it with
parameter averaging techniques to produce pricing
approximations
based on approximations of the second conditional
expectation appearing in (\ref{2.18}) below,
a special case of (\ref{GD}) in our main result.
Bentata and Cont \cite{Ben} have
recently extended Gy\"ongy's result to jump diffusions under a
continuity assumption on the coefficients in the mimicking process and
a nondegeneracy assumption on the covariance or the jump measure of
the mimicking process.

Here we extend Gy\"ongy \cite{G} in two ways.
First, we remove
the conditions of nondegeneracy and boundedness
on the covariance
of the It\^o process to be mimicked,
requiring only integrability
of this process and thereby extending the result to cover
popular stochastic volatility models such as the one due to
Heston \cite{H}.  Second,
we show that the mimicking process can preserve
the joint distribution of certain functionals of the It\^o
process (e.g., running maximum and running average)
at each fixed time.  Our mimicking
process is a weak solution to an SDE, and in the case
of preservation of the joint distribution of functionals
of the It\^o process, the coefficients in this SDE may
depend on the values of
these functionals as well as the current value
of the underlying It\^o process.

The conditions that permit our construction are so weak that the
\gbmarginpar{I reworked this paragraph slightly.  I replaced all
  occurrences of the word ``smooth'' with ``regular.''  There are
  uniqueness results for SDE whose coefficients are not continuous, and
  I read ``smooth'' as $C^\infty$.
  I replaced ``in order to guarantee'' with ``to ensure.''
  I also changed ``conditioning variable'' to ``conditioning
  variables'' and fixed a repetition of the word ``equation'' in the
  last sentence.
solution to the SDE we derive is not necessarily unique.  Uniqueness
results, such as those found in Stroock and Varadhan \cite{SV},
require the conditional expectations determined by the Gy\"ongy-Dupire
formulas (see (\ref{GD}) in this paper) to be sufficiently regular
functions of the conditioning variables. It is difficult to see what
conditions one should impose on the data of our model (the processes
$b$ and $\sigma$ and the updating function $\Phi$ of Theorem
\ref{T2.4}) to ensure such regularity.  Of course, if one
is willing to assume that the coefficients in the mimicking equation
are sufficiently well-behaved, then it is often possible to conclude
that the solution to the mimicking equation is unique.

Finally, we mention an independent body of work
devoted to a problem similar to the one considered here.
If an It\^o process is a submartingale,
Kellerer \cite{Ke} has shown that it can be mimicked by
a Markov process.  More generally, \cite{Ke}
shows that given any set of marginal densities
$p(t,\cdot)$, $t\geq 0$, that have finite first moments
and satisfy
$\int\varphi(y)p(s,y)\,dy\leq\int\varphi(y)p(t,y)$
for every $t\geq s\geq 0$ and every nondecreasing
convex function $\varphi$, there is a Markov submartingale
whose density at each time $t$ is $p(t,\cdot)$.
Madan and Yor \cite{MY} provide constructions of
such Markov processes in three specific cases in which
the first moments of $p(t,\cdot)$ are independent of $t$.
\gbmarginpar{Added Cox and Ekstrom references.
Cox et al.\ \cite{Cox}  and Ekst\"om et al. \cite{Eks}
provide related constructions.
Our results address
\gbmarginpar{Change ``Our result are related to'' to ``address'' to
  avoid repetition of ``related''
the specific case in which
the densities $p(t,\cdot)$ are the marginals
of an It\^o process.  Our mimicking
\gbmarginpar{``processes satisfies'' to ``process satisfies''
process satisfies an SDE,
but because the solution to this equation might not be unique,
we are not able to establish the Markov property
in all cases.   On the other hand, we have the Gy\"ongy-Dupire
formulas for the drift and diffusion coefficients
of our mimicking process.

This paper is based on the first author's Ph.D.\ dissertation \cite{Bru}.
It  is organized as follows.
In Section 2 we present an intuitive discrete-time
example that
illustrates the main ideas of our construction.
In Section 3 we state our main result and provide
some useful
corollaries.  In Sections 4--6
we develop the tools used
in Section 7 to prove the main result.
\vspace{-1.5mm}

\section{Guiding example} \label{DiscreteEx}
\setcounter{equation}{0}
\vspace{-0.7mm}

\gbmarginpar{I messed with the spacing around
  the section title to preserve the page breaks
To motivate
the results that follow, we first
sketch a mimicking result for
discrete-time processes.  This setting
illustrates the main ideas of our
\gbmarginpar{Is ``methodology'' redundant here?
proof methodology without the
technical complications of
continuous time.

Let $\N_0$ denote the set of
nonnegative integers,
let
$\sB(\R)$ denote
the Borel $\sigma$-field on $\R$,
and let $(X_n)_{n\in\N_0}$ denote a
(not necessarily Markov)
stochastic process in discrete time that
takes values in $\mathbb R$.  For each $n \in
\N_0$, we may
\gbmarginpar{``kernal'' to ``kernel''
construct a measurable transition kernel $p_n : \mathbb
R \times \sB(\R) \rightarrow [0,1]$ with the property that $p_n(X_n;
A)$ is a version of $\P[X_{n+1} - X_n \in A \,|\, \sigma(X_n)]$ for each $A
\in \sB(\R)$ and $A \mapsto p_n(x; A)$ is a probability measure for
\gbmarginpar{I added space around all the conditioning bars.
  I didn't add a marginpar for each
  occurrence because there were a lot.
each $x \in \mathbb R$.

After moving to a suitable extension of our
probability space if
necessary, we may construct a process
$Y$ such that $Y_0 = X_0$;
$Y_{n+1} - Y_n$ is conditionally
independent of $\sF_n$ given $Y_n$;
and $p_n(Y_n; A)$ is a version of
$\mathbb P(Y_{n+1} - Y_n \in A
\,|\, \sF_n)$ for each $n \in \mathbb N_0$
and $A \in \sB(\R)$.  It
follows from these properties that
\begin{align*}
  \mathbb E[f(Y_{n+1}) \,|\, \sF_n]
  = \int f(Y_n + x) \, p_n(Y_n; dx),
\end{align*}
so $Y$ is a Markov process.  We also have
\begin{equation*}
    \mathbb E[f(X_{n+1})]
    = \mathbb E \Bigl[ \mathbb E[ f(X_{n+1}) \,|\,\sigma(X_n)] \Bigr]
    = \mathbb E \Bigl[ \int f(X_n + x) \, p_n(X_n; dx)\Bigr],
\end{equation*}
and $Y_0 = X_0$, so an inductive argument shows that $Y_n$ has the
same law as $X_n$ for each $n$.  This is essentially the construction
given by Derman and Kani
\cite{DK2}.

Given a discrete-time process $X$, we
now let $\Xbar_n =
\max_{0\leq i\leq n} X_i$
denote the running maximum of the process $X$.
Although the law of the random variable $Y_n$ constructed above agrees
with the law of $X_n$ for each fixed $n$, the law of the process $Y$
may certainly differ from the law of the process $X$.  In particular,
the law of the pair $(X_n, \Xbar_n)$ may not agree with the law of the
pair $(Y_n, \Ybar_n)$ when $n \geq 1$.  Nevertheless, one can
construct a second process $Z$
such that the two-dimensional
process $(Z, \Zbar)$ is Markov and the joint law of the pair $(Z_n,
\Zbar_n)$ agrees with the joint law of the pair $(X_n, \Xbar_n)$ for
each $n$, as we now show.

We
let $q_n : \R^2 \times \sB(\R) \rightarrow [0,1]$ denote a
transition kernel with the property that $p_n(X_n, \Xbar_n; A)$ is a
version of $\P[X_{n+1} - X_n \in A \,|\,\sigma(X_n, \Xbar_n)]$ for each $A
\in \sB(\R)$.  Moving to another extension of our probability space, we
may construct a process $Z$ such that $Z_0 = X_0$; $Z_{n+1} - Z_n$ is
conditionally independent of $\sF_n$ given $(Z_n, \Zbar_n)$; and
$p_n(Z_n, \Zbar_n; A)$ is a version of $\mathbb P(Z_{n+1} - Z_n \in A
\,|\,\sF_n)$
\gbmarginpar{Changed $n \geq 1$ to $n \in \mathbb N_0$.
for each $n \in \mathbb N_0$.

We define
$\Phi\colon\mathbb{R}^3\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^2$
by $\Phi(e_1, e_2; x)
= (e_1+x, e_2 \vee \,(e_1 + x)) $, so that
$(Z_{n+1}, \Zbar_{n+1})
= \Phi(Z_n, \Zbar_n; Z_{n+1}-Z_n)$.
We may use the function $\Phi$
and the increments of the
process $Z$ to update the state of the process $(Z, \Zbar)$.  One
immediate consequence of this structure is that
\begin{equation*}
  \mathbb E[f(Z_{n+1}, \Zbar_{n+1}) \,|\,\sF_n]
  =  \int f \circ \Phi(Z_{n}, \Zbar_{n}; y) \, q_n(Z_{n}, \Zbar_{n}; dy),
\end{equation*}
so $(Z, \Zbar)$ is a Markov process.  We also have
\begin{equation*}
  \mathbb E[f(X_{n+1}, \Xbar_{n+1})]
  =  \mathbb E\Bigl[\int f \circ \Phi(X_{n}, \Xbar_{n}; y)
                     \, q_n(X_{n}, \Xbar_{n}; dy)\Bigr],
\end{equation*}
so another inductive argument shows that the law of the pair $(Z_n,
\Zbar_n)$ agrees with the law of the pair $(X_n, \Xbar_n)$ for each
$n$.
This paper
extends this
construction to continuous time.

\section{Main result}\label{SecMainResult}
\setcounter{equation}{0}

In order to precisely state our main result,
we need some notation.
The symbol $\calE$ will always denote a
closed subset of a complete separable metric space,
i.e., a Polish space.
 Let $C^\calE$ be the space of
continuous functions from $[0,\infty)$
to $\calE$, endowed with the topology of
uniform convergence on compact
subsets of $[0,\infty)$.
We define the {\em shift operator}
$\Theta\colon C^\calE\times\R\rightarrow
C^\calE$ by
$$
\Theta(x,t)\define x\big((t+\cdot)^+\big),
$$
the {\em stopping operator}
$\nabla\colon C^\calE\times[0,\infty)
\rightarrow C^\calE$ by
$$
\nabla(x,t)\define x(\cdot\wedge t),
$$
and, if $\sE$ is a vector space,
the {\em difference operator}
$\Delta\colon C^\calE\times[0,\infty)
\rightarrow C^\calE$ by
$$
\Delta(x,t)\define x(t+\cdot)-x(t).
$$
In contrast to usual practice, here the
shift operator
can shift paths to the right because
$t$ can be negative,
and in this case, the shifted path takes
the value $x(0)$ on $[0,-t]$.
The difference
operator actually
maps into $C_0^\calE$, the space of
continuous functions from
$[0,\infty)$ to $\calE$ with initial
condition zero.
If $\calE=\R^d$ for some integer $d$, we write
$C^d$ and $C^d_0$ rather than $C^{\R^d}$
and $C^{\R^d}_0$.

Fix a Polish space $\calE$, fix a positive
integer $d$, and
define $\OmegaEd\define\calE\times C_0^d$.
We endow $\OmegaEd$
with the product topology.
We denote a generic element of $\OmegaEd$
by $\omega=(e,x)$
and define the random variable $E(e,x)=e$
and the $\R^d$-valued
process $X(e,x)=x$.  For a random time $T$,
we use the notation $X^T$ to denote the process $X$ stopped at $T$,
i.e.,
\be\label{2.4}
X^T_t(\omega)=X_{t\wedge T(\omega)}(\omega)
=\nabla_t\big(X(\omega),T(\omega)\big),
\quad t\geq 0.
\ee
\begin{definition}\label{D2.1}
We say that
$\Phi\colon\OmegaEd\rightarrow C^\calE$
is an {\em updating
function} provided
\bea
\Phi_0(e,x)&=&e,\quad e\in\calE,\label{2.5}\\
\Phi^t(e,x)&=&\Phi^t\big(e,\nabla(x,t)\big),
\quad t\geq 0,\,\,
e\in\calE,\,\,x\in C_0^d,\label{2.6}\\
\Theta\big(\Phi(e,x),t\big)
&=&\Phi\big(\Phi_t(e,x),\Delta(x,t)\big),\quad
t\geq 0,\,\,e\in\calE,\,\,x\in C_0^d.\label{2.7}
\eea
\end{definition}

In other words, $\Phi$ takes an initial
condition in $\calE$ (see (\ref{2.5}))
and a path in $C_0^d$ and
generates a path in $C^\calE$.
Property (\ref{2.6}) says that the path
$\Phi(e,x)$ stopped
at $t$ depends only on the initial condition $e$
and the path of $x$ stopped at $t$.  This is
a non-anticipative
property.  Property (\ref{2.7}) is a type
of Markov property,
but on a path-by-path basis without the
presence of a probability
measure. It implies that the path of
$\Phi(e,x)$ from time $t$
onward depends only on the value of the
path at time $t$
and the increments of $x$ from time $t$
onward.  Using
the characterization of the Markov property
as independence
of the future and past given the present,
it is easily verified that
if $\xi$ is a continuous $\R^d$-valued Markov
process, and if
for each $t$ the value of $\xi_t$
can be deduced from the value
of $\Phi_t(\xi_0,\xi-\xi_0)$, then $\Phi(\xi_0,\xi-\xi_0)$ is
also Markov.

\bex[Process itself]\label{Ex2.3}
{\rm
A trivial case of an updating
function is obtained if we let
$\calE=\R^d$, $\OmegaEd=\calE\times C_0^d$, and
$\Phi(e,x)=e+x$ for $e\in\R^d$ and $x\in C_0^d$.
If $\xi$ is a continuous
$\R^d$-valued Markov process and we
represent $\xi$ as
$(\xi_0,\xi-\xi_0)\in\calE\times C_0^d$,
then $\Phi_t(\xi_0,\xi-\xi_0)=\xi_t$
and $\Phi(\xi_0,\xi-\xi_0)=\xi$ is Markov.
}
\eex

\bex[Integral-to-date]\label{IntegralEx}
{\rm
Let $\calE=\R^2$ and $\OmegaE1=\calE\times
C_0^1$.  We intepret a point
\gbmarginpar{Changed $(e_1, e_2, x)$ to $(e1, e_2; x)$
  in Ex3.3 and Ex3.4.  This makes the notation
  consistent with the previous example.
$(e_1,e_2;\,x)\in\Omega^{\sE,1}$
as a path $e_1+x$ with initial condition
$e_1+x(0)=e_1$
and the inital
value of a running integral given
by $e_2$.  It is then easy to check
that
$$
\Phi_t(e_1,e_2;\,x)
=\Bigl(e_1+x(t), \; e_2
+ \int_0^t \big(e_1+x(s)\big) \, ds\Bigr)
$$
is an updating function.
}
\eex

\bex[Maximum-to-date]\label{Ex2.2}
{\rm
Let
$\calE=\{(e_1,e_2)\in\R^2:e_1\leq e_2\}$
and $\OmegaE1=\calE\times C_0^1$.
We regard the generic element
$(e_1,e_2;\,x)\in\Omega^{\sE,1}$
as a path $e_1+x$ with initial
condition $e_1+x(0)=e_1$
and the time-zero maximum-to-date $e_2$.
Given such a triple,
the value of the path at a later time
$t$ and the maximum-to-date at that
time $t$ are $e_1+x(t)$ and
$e_2\vee\max_{0\leq s\leq t}\big(e_1+x(s)\big)$,
respectively.  We thus define
$$
\Phi_t(e_1,e_2;\,x)
=\big(e_1+x(t), \; e_2\vee
\max_{0\leq s\leq t}\big(e_1+x(s)\big)
\big).
$$
It is straightforward to verify that
$\Phi$ is an updating function.
If $\xi$ is a continuous real-valued Markov process,
then
$\Phi_t(\xi_0,M_0;\,\xi-\xi_0)
=(\xi_t, M_0\vee\max_{0\leq s\leq t}\xi_s)$
is also Markov,
where $M_0$ is any random variable
satisfying $M_0\geq \xi_0$ almost surely.
}
\eex

As a final extremal example,
we give an updating function that
records the entire history of the path.
\bex[Path-to-date]\label{Ex2.4} {\rm Define
$\calE=\big\{(s,x)\in [0,\infty)\times C^d;
x\mbox{ is constant on }[s,\infty)\big\}$,
\gbmarginpar{Changed $((s,x),y)$ to $(s,x;\,y))$ in Ex3.5 and
  added a little space before the first $\nabla$ in the
  display.
define $\OmegaEd=\calE\times C_0^d$, and set
$$
\Phi_t(s,x;\,y)=
\Big(s+t,\;\nabla\big(\nabla(x,s)
+\Theta(y,-s),s+t\big)\Big),\quad x\in C^d,
s\in[0,\infty), y\in C_0^d.
$$
Given paths $x\in C^d$ and $y\in C_0^d$
and a time $s\geq 0$,
$\nabla(x,s)+\Theta(y,-s)$
is the path that follows $x$ on
$[0,s]$ with
$y$ appended after time $s$.  The second component
of $\Phi_t$
is this path stopped at time $s+t$.
The first component
of $\Phi_t$ is the time $s+t$ at which
this path is stopped.
As $t$ marches forward, the second component
of the
operator $\Phi$ applied to $(s,x;\,y)$
appends more and more of the path $y$ to
the path $x$,
always appending at time $s$.  It is tedious
but straightforward to check that $\Phi$
is an updating function. For any continuous
$\R^d$-valued process $\xi$, we have
\be\label{2.12a}
\Phi_t(0,\xi^0;\,\xi-\xi_0)=(t,\xi^t),
\quad t\geq 0,
\ee
where we recall from (\ref{2.4}) that
$\xi^t$ is the process
$\xi$ stopped at $t$.
\gbmarginpar{Removed ``We are using $\Phi$ to keep track of the
  path-to-date. Even if we are using a probability measure under which
  $\xi$ is not Markov, the process in (\ref{2.12a}) is Markov.''  This
  may not be true if the filtration is larger than the filtration
  generated by $\xi$, Moreover, when the filtration is generated by
  $\xi$ this statement is essentially a tautology.
}
\eex

\bt[Main result]\label{T2.4}
Suppose an $\R^d$-valued process $Y$ is given by
\be\label{2.10}
Y_t=\int_0^tb_s\,ds + \int_0^t\sigma_s\,dW_s,\quad t\geq 0,
\ee
where $W$ is an $\R^r$-valued Brownian motion under some probability
measure $\P$, $b$ is an $\R^d$-valued process adapted to a filtration
under which $W$ is a Brownian motion, and $\sigma$ is a $d\times r$
matrix-valued process adapted to the same filtration as $b$.  Assume
that $\E\int_0^t\big(\|b_s\|
+\|\sigma_s\sigma_s^{tr}\|\big)\,ds<\infty$ for $t\geq 0$.  Let
$\calE$ be a Polish space, define $\OmegaEd\define\calE\times C_0^d$,
let $\Phi\colon\OmegaEd\rightarrow C^{\calE}$ be a continuous updating
function, and let $Z$ be a continuous, $\calE$-valued process
satisfying $Z=\Phi(Z_0,Y)$.  Then there exists a nonrandom
$\R^d$-valued measurable function $\bhat$ and a nonrandom $d\times d$
matrix-valued measurable function $\sigmahat$, both defined on
$[0,\infty)\times \calE$, and there exists a Lebesgue-null set
$N\subset[0,\infty)$, so that
\be\label{GD}
\bhat(t,Z_t)=
\E[b_t\,|\, Z_t],\quad \sigmahat(t,Z_t)\sigmahat^{tr}(t,Z_t)=
\E[\sigma_t\sigma_t^{tr}\,|\, Z_t], \quad t\in N^c.
\ee
Furthermore, there exists a filtered probability space $(\Omegahat,
\sFhat,\{\sFhat_t\}_{t\geq 0},\Phat)$ that supports a continuous
$\R^d$-valued adapted process $\Yhat$, a continuous $\calE$-valued
adapted process $\Zhat$, and a $d$-dimensional Brownian motion $\What$
satisfying
\bea
\Yhat_t
=
\int_0^t\bhat(s,\Zhat_s)\,ds
+\int_0^t\sigmahat(s,\Zhat_s)\,d\What_s,
\quad \Zhat = \Phi(\Zhat_0,\Yhat),
\quad t\geq 0,\label{2.14}
\eea
and such that for each $t\geq 0$, the distribution of $\Zhat_t$ under
$\Phat$ agrees with the distribution of $Z_t$ under $\P$.  \et

Although both $Y$ in (\ref{2.10})
\gbmarginpar{Removing your marginpar
  above ``Although'' changes the page
  breaks on this page, but not the next page.
and $\Yhat$ in (\ref{2.14}) are $d$-dimensional
processes, the ``state'' $\Zhat$ of the system
in (\ref{2.14}) can be of a much lower
dimension that the state process
needed to describe (\ref{2.10}).
In (\ref{2.10})
the processes $b$ and $\sigma$ are typically
given by stochastic differential equations
driven by additional Brownian motions not
mentioned in the statement of the theorem.
The process $\Zhat$ is typically the
process $\Yhat$ itself augmented by
some functional of the path of $\Yhat$.
We give examples below.  Indeed, the
remainder of this section
illustrates the applications of Theorem
\ref{T2.4}.
In this section we also show
by example that (\ref{2.14}) can have multiple
solutions
and discuss
conditions that guarantee uniqueness.
The subsequent sections are
devoted to the proof of
Theorem \ref{T2.4}.

As a first application, we take $Y = X - X_0$ and $Z=X$ in Theorem
\ref{T2.4} and use the updating function of Example \ref{Ex2.3}.  We
then have the following corollary, which
is the result obtained by
Gy\"{o}ngy \cite{G}, but here without the
boundedness and
nondegeneracy
assumptions of \cite{G}.

\bcor[Process itself]\label{C2.6}
Suppose an $\R^d$-valued process $X$ is given by
\be\label{2.11gb}
X_t = X_0 + \int_0^tb_s\,ds
+\int_0^t\sigma_s\,dW_s,\quad t\geq 0,
\ee
where $W$, $\P$, $b$ and $\sigma$ are as in Theorem \ref{T2.4}.  Then
there exists a nonrandom $\R^d$-valued measurable function $\bhat$ and
a nonrandom $d\times d$ matrix-valued measurable function $\sigmahat$,
both defined on $[0,\infty)\times \R^d$, and there exists a
Lebesgue-null set $N$, so that
\be\label{2.18}
\bhat(t,X_t)=
\E[b_t\,|\, X_t],\quad
\sigmahat(t,X_t)\sigmahat^{tr}(t,X_t)=
\E\big[\sigma_t\sigma_t^{tr}\,\big|\,X_t\big],
\quad t\in N^c.
\ee
Furthermore,
there exists a filtered probability space
$(\Omegahat,\sFhat,\{\sFhat_t\}_{t\geq 0},\Phat)$
that supports a continuous
$\R^d$-valued adapted process $\Xhat$ and
a $d$-dimensional Brownian motion
$\What$ satisfying
\be\label{2.19}
\Xhat_t=\Xhat_0+\int_0^t\bhat(s,\Xhat_s)\,ds
+\int_0^t\sigmahat(s,\Xhat_s)\,d\What_s,
\quad t\geq 0,
\ee
and such that for each $t\geq 0$,
the distribution of $\Xhat_t$
under $\Phat$ agrees with the distribution
of $X_t$ under $\P$.
\ecor

Taking $Y = X - X_0$ and $Z_t = (X_t, A_t)$,
and using the
updating function in Example \ref{IntegralEx}, we
obtain the following corollary about the
distribution of a process and its running integral.

\bcor[Integral-to-date]\label{IntegralCor}
Suppose a real-valued process $X$ is given by
\eqref{2.11gb}
where $W$, $\P$, $b$ and $\sigma$
are as in Theorem \ref{T2.4} with $d=r=1$.
Let $A$ be a continuous process such that
$$
A_t=A_0 + \int_0^t X_s \, ds,
\quad t\geq 0.
$$
Then there exists a
nonrandom real-valued measurable
function $\bhat$ and a
nonrandom $[0,\infty)$-valued
measurable function $\sigmahat$,
both defined on
$[0,\infty)\times \mathbb R^2$,
and there exists a Lebesgue-null
set $N$, such that
$$
\bhat(t,X_t,A_t)=
\E[b_t\,|\,X_t,A_t],\quad
\sigmahat^2(t,X_t,A_t)=
\E[\sigma_t^2\,|\,X_t,A_t],
\quad t\in N^c.
$$
Furthermore,
there exists a filtered probability space
$(\Omegahat,\sFhat,\{\sFhat_t\}_{t\geq 0},
\Phat)$ that supports continuous
real-valued adapted processes $\Xhat$ and $\Ahat$
and a real-valued Brownian motion
\gbmarginpar{Added label to equation}
$\What$ satisfying
\begin{equation} \label{eq:integraltodate}
\begin{aligned}
\Xhat_t
&=
\Xhat_0+\int_0^t\bhat(s,\Xhat_s, \Ahat_s)\,ds
+\int_0^t\sigmahat(s,\Xhat_s,\Ahat_s)\,d\What_s,
\quad t\geq 0,\\
\Ahat_t
&=
\Ahat_0 + \int_0^t \Xhat_s \, ds,
\quad t\geq 0,
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
and such that for each $t\geq0$,
the distribution of the pair $(\Xhat_t, \Ahat_t)$
under $\Phat$ agrees with the distribution
of the pair $(X_t, A_t)$ under $\P$.
\ecor

Taking $Y = X - X_0$ and $Z_t = (X_t, M_t)$,
and using the
updating function in Example \ref{Ex2.2}, we
obtain the following corollary about the
distribution of a process and its running maximum.

\bcor[Maximum-to-date]\label{C2.7}
Suppose a real-valued process $X$ is given by
\eqref{2.11gb}
where $W$, $\P$, $b$ and $\sigma$
are as in Theorem \ref{T2.4} with $d=r=1$.
Let $M_0$ be a random variable
satisfying $M_0\geq X_0$ almost surely
and define
$$
M_t=M_0\vee\max_{0\leq s\leq t}X_s,
\quad t\geq 0.
$$
Then there exists a
nonrandom real-valued measurable
function $\bhat$ and a
nonrandom $[0,\infty)$-valued
measurable function $\sigmahat$,
both defined on
$[0,\infty)\times \mathbb R^2$,
and there exists a Lebesgue-null
set $N$, such that
$$
\bhat(t,X_t,M_t)=
\E[b_t\,|\,X_t,M_t],\quad
\sigmahat^2(t,X_t,M_t)=
\E[\sigma_t^2\,|\,X_t,M_t],
\quad t\in N^c.
$$
Furthermore,
there exists a filtered probability space
$(\Omegahat,\sFhat,\{\sFhat_t\}_{t\geq 0},\Phat)$
that supports continuous
real-valued adapted processes $\Xhat$ and $\Mhat$
and a real-valued Brownian motion
$\What$ satisfying
\begin{equation} \label{eq:runningmax}
  \begin{aligned}
    \Xhat_t
    &= \Xhat_0+\int_0^t\bhat(s,\Xhat_s, \Mhat_s)\,ds
       +\int_0^t\sigmahat(s,\Xhat_s,\Mhat_s)\,d\What_s,
       \quad t\geq 0,
    \\
    \Mhat_t &= \Mhat_0\vee\max_{0\leq s\leq t}\Xhat_s, \quad t\geq 0,
  \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
and such that for each $t\geq0$,
the distribution of the pair $(\Xhat_t, \Mhat_t)$
under $\Phat$ agrees with the distribution
of the pair $(X_t, M_t)$ under $\P$.
\ecor

Taking $Y = X - X_0$ and $Z_t = (t,X^t)$,
and using the
updating function in Example \ref{Ex2.4}, we
obtain the following corollary, which states that
every It\^o process with integrable drift and
covariance is a weak solution to an
SDE with path-dependent coefficients.

\bcor[Path-to-date]
Suppose a real-valued process $X$ is given by
\eqref{2.11gb}
where $W$, $\P$, $b$ and $\sigma$
are as in Theorem \ref{T2.4}.
Then there exist
path-dependent functionals $\bhat$ and
$\sigmahat$, both defined on $[0,\infty) \times
C^d$, with $\bhat$ taking values in $\R^d$ and
$\sigmahat$ taking values in the space of $d\times
d$ matrices, and a Lebesgue-null set $N$ such that
$$
\bhat(t,X^t)=
\E[b_t\,|\,X^t],\quad
\sigmahat(t,X^t)\sigmahat^{tr}(t,X^t)=
\E[\sigma_t\sigma_t^{tr}\,|\,X^t],
\quad t\in N^c.
$$
Furthermore,
there exists a filtered probability space
$(\Omegahat,\sFhat,\{\sFhat_t\}_{t\geq 0},\Phat)$
that supports a continuous
$\R^d$-valued adapted process $\Xhat$ and
a $d$-dimensional Brownian motion
$\What$ satisfying
$$
\Xhat_t=\Xhat_0+\int_0^t\bhat(s,\Xhat^s)\,ds
+\int_0^t\sigmahat(s,\Xhat^s)\,d\What_s,
\quad t\geq 0,
$$
and such that $\Xhat$ has the same distribution
under $\Phat$ as $X$ has under $\P$.
\ecor

We close this section with a brief discussion of the nonuniqueness
that can arise in equation (\ref{2.14}) of Theorem \ref{T2.4} and its
relationship to the strong Markov property.  We first provide a simple
example within the context of Corollary \ref{C2.6}, where $X$ and
$Z$ are the same process.

\bex[Nonuniqueness]\label{Ex2.8}
{\rm Let $d=1$ and $b=0$ in Corollary \ref{C2.6} and let
$X_t=\int_0^t\sigma_s\,dW_s$,
where
$\sigma_s
=\ind_{(1,\infty)}(s)\ind_{\{W_1>0\}}$.
Then
$X_t=\ind_{(1,\infty)}(t)
\ind_{\{W_1>0\}}(W_t-W_1)$.
From (\ref{2.18}) we see that
$\sigmahat(t,y)=0$
for $0\leq t\leq 1$, and for $t>1$,
$$
\sigmahat^2(t,y)=\E[\sigma_t^2\,|\,X_t=y]
=\left\{\begin{array}{ll}
1,&\mbox{if }y\neq 0,\\
0,&\mbox{if }y=0.
\end{array}\right.
$$
Both $\Xhat^1_t\equiv 0$ and
$\Xhat^2_t=\ind_{(1,\infty)}(t)(W_t-W_1)$
are solutions of  (\ref{2.19}).
The weak solution $\Xhat$ that has
the same one-dimensional distributions
as $X$ is obtained by an initial randomization
that is independent of $W$
and determines whether $\Xhat$
agrees with $\Xhat^1$ or
$\Xhat^2$, each of these
events having probability $\frac12$.
This process is Markov, but not strong
Markov, as can be seen by considering the stopping
time that is the first time after time $2$
that zero is reached.
$\endproof$
}
\eex


The previous example shows that the mimicking
process may not be strong
Markov.  Nevertheless, if we are willing to
impose further conditions
on the coefficients $\bhat$ and $\sigmahat$
appearing in
Theorem~\ref{T2.4}, then we can often
conclude that
the solution to (\ref{2.19}) is unique in law and
strong Markov.
In particular,
if we assume that
$\bhat$ appearing
in Corollary~\ref{C2.6} is
bounded and measurable and
that
$\sigmahat \sigmahat^{tr}$ is bounded,
strictly positive-definite, and continuous, then
the results of Stroock and Varadhan \cite{SV}
ensure that the
mimicking process satisfying (\ref{2.19})
in Corollary~\ref{C2.6} is
unique in law and
strong Markov with respect
to its natural filtration.  In fact, more recent
results of Krylov \cite{Kry4} imply
that the mimicking process
in Corollary~\ref{C2.6} is
unique in law and strong Markov when $\bhat$ is
bounded and measurable and
$\sigmahat \sigmahat^{tr}$ is bounded,
locally uniformly positive-definite, and
continuous in the sense of
vanishing mean oscillation.  If we
restrict attention
to the one-dimensional case, then the
mimicking process
in Corollary~\ref{C2.6} is
unique in law and strong Markov when $\bhat$ is
bounded and measurable, and $\sigmahat$ is bounded,
locally uniformly
positive, and measurable
\gbmarginpar{Changed ``7.33'' to ``7.3.3.''
(Exercise~7.3.3 of \cite{SV2}).

Similarly, Theorem~5.10 of
\cite{Bru2} asserts that
the solution to \eqref{eq:integraltodate}
is uniquely determined in law
when $\bhat$ is
\gbmarginpar{Reworked this paragraph to clarify what
  is shown in \cite{Bru2}.
bounded and measurable and $\sigmahat$ is bounded,
strictly positive, and
continuous.  It then follows that the mimicking processes
in Corollary~\ref{IntegralCor} possesses the strong
Markov property when these conditions hold.
The two-dimensional
process $(\Xhat, \Ahat)$ is
degenerate, so the results of Stroock
and Varadhan \cite{SV,SV2} do not apply.

We observe finally that the path
functional
$x \mapsto \max_{s \in [0,t]} x(s)$ is Lipschitz
continuous for each fixed $t\geq 0$.  This implies
that pathwise
uniqueness holds for the mimicking
equation \eqref{eq:runningmax}
in Corollary~\ref{C2.7} when $\bhat$ and $\sigmahat$ are
bounded and locally Lipschitz continuous.
As a result, it is easy to
check that the process $(\Xhat, \Mhat)$ in
Corollary~\ref{C2.7} is strong Markov
under these conditions.

To summarize, we cannot conclude
in general that the mimicking process
$\Zhat$
in Theorem~\ref{T2.4} is unique in law and
strong Markov.
In many cases
of interest, it is
possible to identify conditions
that may be imposed on the mimicking
equation to ensure that the solution
is unique and that the mimicking
process possesses the strong Markov property.
However, these
conditions vary from case to case,
and depend in an essential way on
the structure of the updating function.

\section{Concatenated measure}\label{SConMea}
\setcounter{equation}{0}
\setcounter{theorem}{0}

In this section we begin with
a measure $\P$
and a partition $\Pi$ of
$[0,\infty)$ and construct a
{\em concatenated measure}.
This is the continuous-time analogue
of the measure induced on path space
by the process $Y$ or the pair
$(Z, \overline{Z})$ in Section \ref{DiscreteEx}.
We use the notation introduced
at the beginning of
Section \ref{SecMainResult}.
On the space $\OmegaEd=\calE\times C_0^d$,
we introduce
the $\sigma$-field
$\sFEd\define\frakE\otimes\sigma(X)$ and the
filtration
$\sFEd_t\define\frakE\otimes\sigma(X^t)$,
$t\geq 0$,
where $\frakE$ is the Borel
$\sigma$-field in $\calE$.

\begin{definition}\label{D3.2}
Let $0=T_0\leq T_1\leq\dots\leq T_n$
be a sequence of
finite (for {\em every} $\omega$)
$\{\sFEd_t\}_{t\geq 0}$-stopping times and let
$\{\sG_i\}_{i=0}^n$ be a collection of
$\sigma$-fields satisfying
$\sG_i\subset\sFEd_{T_i}$ for
$i=0,\dots,n$.  Set $T_{n+1}=\infty$,
set $\sH_0=\sFEd_0$, and define
$\sH_{i+1}\define
\sG_i\vee\sigma
\big(\Delta(X^{T_{i+1}},T_i)\big)$,
$i=0,1,\dots,n$.
We say that
$\Pi\define(T_i,\sG_i)_{i=0}^n$
is an {\em extended partition} provided
\bdes
\item[(a)]
$T_{i+1}-T_i\in\sG_i\vee
\sigma\big(\Delta(X,T_i)\big),\quad
i=0,1,\dots,n-1$,
\item[(b)]
$\sG_i\subset\sH_i,\quad i=0,1,\dots,n$.
\edes
\end{definition}

\br\label{R3.2}
{\rm
Because $T_{i+1}-T_i$ is
$\sFEd_{T_{i+1}}$-measurable
and $\sFEd_{T_{i+1}}=\frakE\otimes
\sigma(X^{T_{i+1}})$,
condition (a) in Definition 3.1
is equivalent to the
apparently stronger condition
\bdes
\item[(a$'$)]
$T_{i+1}-T_i\in\sH_{i+1},\quad i=0,1,\dots,n-1$.
\edes
Because $\sG_i\subset\sFEd_{T_i}
\subset\sFEd_{T_{i+1}}$
and $\sigma(\Delta(X^{T_{i+1}},T_i))
\subset\sFEd_{T_{i+1}}$,
we have $\sH_{i+1}\subset\sFEd_{T_{i+1}}$, or equivalently
\be\label{3.1a}
\sH_{i}\subset\sFEd_{T_{i}},
\quad i=0,1,\dots,n,n+1.
\ee
$\endproof$
}
\er

An extended partition is a model
for observing and partially forgetting
information over time.  Partial forgetting
occurs in Section \ref{DiscreteEx} when
we condition on the value of a process
at time $n$ rather than on $\sF_n$.
With an extended partition, at time $T_i$
we retain the information in $\sG_i$ as
we move forward into the interval $[T_i,T_{i+1}]$,
but carry no other
information from $\sFEd_{T_i}$ forward.  We
then observe increments in
$X$ over the interval $[T_i,T_{i+1}]$,
so that the information we have
at time $T_{i+1}$ is $\sH_{i+1}$.  This
information is sufficient to
tell us the length of time $T_{i+1}-T_i$
we conduct the observations.
We then remember
only the information in the
sub-$\sigma$-field $\sG_{i+1}$ of the
information in
$\sH_{i+1}$ as we go forward into the
interval $[T_{i+1},T_{i+2}]$.

\subsection{Existence and uniqueness
of concatenated measure}\label{SExisUniq}

\bt[$n$-fold concatenation] \label{T3.3}
Let $\P$ be a probability measure on
\gbmarginpar{Removed ``the space''
$(\OmegaEd,\sFEd)$,
and let $(T_i,\sG_i)_{i=0}^n$
be an extended partition.
Then there exists a unique measure
$\Pc$ satisfying
\bea
\Pc[A]&=&\P[A],\quad A\in\sH_i,
\,\,i=0,1,\dots,n+1,\label{3.2}\\
\Pc\big[B\,\big|\,\sFEd_{T_i}\big]
&=&
\P\big[B\,\big|\,\sG_i\big],\quad
B\in\sH_{i+1},\,\,i=0,1,\dots,n.\label{3.3}
\eea
We interpret (\ref{3.3}) to mean that
every $\P$-version of
$\P[B\,|\,\sG_i]$ is a $\Pc$-version of
$\Pc[B\,|\,\sFEd_{T_i}]$.
\et

\begin{example}[Simple concatenated
measure]\label{SimpExPart1}
{\rm
Let $\sE=\{0\}$, so that
$\Omega^{\sE,1}$ is isomorphic to $C_0^1$.
Then $\sF^{\sE,1}_0$ is the trivial
$\sigma$-algebra $\{\emptyset,C_0^1\}$.
We consider the extended
\gbmarginpar{I changed $\Pi=(T_i,\sG_i)_{i=1}^{0}$
  to $\Pi=(T_i,\sG_i)_{i=0}^{1}$
partition $\Pi=(T_i,\sG_i)_{i=0}^{1}$
with $\sG_0=\sG_1=\{\emptyset,C_0^1\}$
and $T_0=0$, $T_1=1$, and, by convention,
$T_2=\infty$.  Then $\sH_0=\sF^{\sE,1}_0$,
$\sH_1=\sF^{\sE,1}_1=\sigma(X(t), 0\leq t\leq 1)$,
and $\sH_2=\sigma(X(t)-X(1), t\geq 1)$.
We define four elements of $C_0^1$
\gbmarginpar{Changed $\omega^1(t)=0$ to $\omega^0(t)=0$.
by
$\omega^0(t)=0$, $\omega^1(t)=t$,
$\omega^2(t)=t\wedge 1$ and $\omega^3(t)=(t-1)^+$
for $t\geq 0$.
Let $\delta^i$ be the probability measure
on $C_0^1$ assigning probability $1$
to $\omega^i$, and set
$\P=(\delta^0+\delta^1)/2$.
The sets
\gbmarginpar{Added a little more space before each $\forall$.}
$$
A_0=
\{x\in C_0^1:x(t)=0\;\;\forall t\in[0,1] \}
\mbox{ and }
A_1=
\{x\in C_0^1:x(t)=t\;\;\forall t\in[0,1]\}
$$
are in $\sH_1=\sF^{\sE,1}_1$
and $\P(A_0)=\P(A_1)=\frac12$.
According to (\ref{3.2}), we must also have
$\Pc(A_0)=\Pc(A_1)=\frac12$.
The sets
\beas
B_0
&=&
\{x\in C_0^1:x(t)-x(1)=0\;\;\forall t\in[1,\infty)\},\\
B_1
&=&
\{x\in C_0^1:x(t)-x(1)=t-1\;\;\forall t\in[1,\infty)\}
\eeas
are in $\sH_2$, and
\gbmarginpar{I reversed the order of the equation.
(\ref{3.3}) implies that
$$
\Pc[B_0\,|\,\sF^{\sE,1}_1]
=\P[B_0\,|\,\sG_1]
=\P[B_0]
=\frac12.
$$
Integrating this equation over $A_1$
with respect to $\Pc$,
we see that
\gbmarginpar{I reversed the order of $A_1$ and $B_0$.
$$
\frac14=\Pc(A_1\cap B_0)=\Pc(\omega^2).
$$
Considering all combinations of $A_j$
and $B_k$, we conclude that
$\Pc(\omega^i)=\frac14$ for $i=0,1,2,3$,
i.e., $\Pc=(\delta_0+\delta_1+\delta_2+\delta_3)/4$.
$\endproof$
}
\end{example}

The remainder of this subsection is devoted
\gbmarginpar{This paragraph has changed significantly.  I removed the
  $\oplus$ notation, so we only use $\otimes$.  This makes everything
  sync up with the notation in Stroock and Varadhan and allows us to
  abbreviate the proof of Prop. 4.6.
to the proof of Theorem \ref{T3.3}.  Let $\frakC^d$ denote the Borel
$\sigma$-field in $C^d$ and let $\frakC_0^d$ denote the trace
$\sigma$-field in $C_0^d$.  We first concatenate a deterministic
initial path and a probability measure at a deterministic time.  Given
a fixed point $\omegabar=(\ebar,\xbar)\in\OmegaEd$, a time $t \geq 0$,
and a probability measure $\Q$ on $(\OmegaEd,\sFEd)$, let
$\Psi_{\omegabar,t}\colon \OmegaEd\rightarrow\OmegaEd$ denote the
function
\begin{equation} \label{eq:1}
  \Psi_{\omegabar,t}(e,x)=\bigl(\ebar,\;\nabla(\xbar,t)+x-\nabla(x,t)\bigr),
\end{equation}
and set $\delta_{\omegabar}\otimes_t\Q =
\Q\circ\Psi^{-1}_{\omegabar,t}$.  The reader can easily check that the
measure $\delta_{\omegabar}\otimes_t\Q$ is uniquely determined by the
properties
\begin{gather}
  \label{eq:2}
  (\delta_{\omegabar}\otimes_t\Q)
    [E = \ebar, X_s = \xbar(s) \;\; \forall s \leq t] = 1,
  \\
  \label{eq:3}
  (\delta_{\omegabar}\otimes_t\Q)[\Delta(X, t) \in A]
    = \Q[\Delta(X, t) \in A], \quad \forall A \in \frakC_0^d.
\end{gather}
If $\Q[X_t=\xbar(t)] = 1$, $\calE = \R^d$, and we identify $\OmegaEd$
with $C^d$ in the natural way, then this notation reduces to the
construction given in Lemma 6.1.1 of \cite{SV2}.


In the next step, we concatenate an initial probability
\gbmarginpar{I added this sentence.
measure and a probability kernel at a stopping time.

\begin{definition}\label{D3.4}
Let $(\Omega',\sF')$ and $(\Omega'',\sF'')$ be
\gbmarginpar{I modified this definition.  There is
  no reason to mention $\sG'$.
measurable spaces.
We say that a function
$Q\colon\Omega'\times\sF''\rightarrow[0,1]$
is a
{probability kernel from $(\Omega',\sF')$ to
$(\Omega'',\sF'')$} provided
\bdes
\item[(a)]
$Q(\omega',A'')$ is a $\sF'$-measurable
function of $\omega'\in\Omega'$
for each $A''\in\sF''$,
\item[(b)]
$Q(\omega',\cdot)$ is a probability measure on
$(\Omega'',\sF'')$ for each $\omega'\in\Omega'$.
\edes
\end{definition}

\gbmarginpar{I removed a descriptive paragraph
  which described the (now gone) $\oplus$ construction
  in words.  I believe the sentence prior to the previous
  definition gives essentially the same information.
  Whereas $\oplus$ takes a measure on $C_0^d$ as its second argument,
  $\otimes$ takes a measure on $\OmegaEd$ and has the differencing
  built in.

\bp\label{P3.5}
Let $\P$ be a probability measure on
$(\OmegaEd,\sFEd)$, let $T$ be a finite (for every
$\omega$) $\{\sFEd_t\}_{t\geq 0}$-stopping time,
and let $Q$ be a probability
kernel from $(\OmegaEd,\sFEd_T)$ to
$(\OmegaEd,\sFEd)$.  Then there exists a
unique probability measure $\P\otimes_TQ$ on
$(\OmegaEd,\sFEd)$ such that
\bdes
\item[(a)]
$\P\otimes_TQ[A]=\P[A],\quad A\in\sFEd_T$,
\item[(b)]
the random variable
$\omega\mapsto\big(\delta_{\omega}
\otimes_{T(\omega)}
Q(\omega,\cdot)\big)[F]$
is a version of the conditional probability
$(\P\otimes_TQ)[F\,|\,\sFEd_T]$ for all $F\in\sFEd$.
\edes
\ep

\noi {\sc Proof:}
\gbmarginpar{The statement and proof of Prop 4.6 have changed.
  It is now shorter and uses the
  result from Stroock and Varadhan in a effort to address the
  referee's concerns about rederiving known results.
When the initial condition $Q(\omegabar,
\{X_{T(\omegabar)}=X_{T(\omegabar)}(\omegabar)\}) = 1$ holds for each
$\omegabar \in \OmegaEd$, the result follows in the same way as
Theorem~6.1.2 of \cite{SV2}.  To handle the general case, we modify
the initial segment of each path to ensure that the proper
initial condition holds.  Let $\Psi_{\omegabar,t}$ be defined as in
\eqref{eq:1} and set $\Qhat(\omegabar, \cdot\,) = Q(\omegabar,
\cdot\,) \circ \Psi^{-1}_{\omegabar, T(\omegabar)}$.  The map
$(\omegabar, \omega) \mapsto \Psi_{\omegabar, T(\omegabar)}(\omega)$
is $\sFEd_T \otimes \sFEd / \sFEd$-measurable, so $\Qhat$ is a
probability kernel from $(\OmegaEd,\sFEd_T)$ to $(\OmegaEd,\sFEd)$.
It follows from the definition of $\Psi$ that $\Qhat(\omegabar,
\{X^{T(\omegabar)}=X^{T(\omegabar)}(\omegabar)\}) = 1$ for each $\omegabar \in
\OmegaEd$, so we may apply the previous case to conclude that there
exists a unique measure $\P\otimes_T \widehat Q$ such that (a) and (b)
hold when $Q$ is replaced with $\widehat Q$.  But the operator $\omega
\mapsto \Psi_{\omegabar,t}(\omega)$ is idempotent, so
$\delta_{\omegabar} \otimes_{T(\omegabar)} Q(\omegabar,\cdot) =
\delta_{\omegabar} \otimes_{T(\omegabar)} \widehat Q(\omegabar,\cdot)$
for each $\omegabar \in \OmegaEd$, and $\P\otimes_T Q = \P\otimes_T
\widehat Q$ is in fact the unique measure which satisfies (a) and (b).
$\endproof$

\vspace{\baselineskip}
We now begin concatenating probability measures.
\gbmarginpar{I added a sentence (and baselineskip) before Cor. 4.7.

\bcor[Two-fold concatenation]\label{C3.6}
Let $\P_1$ and $\P_2$ be probability measures
on $\OmegaEd$, let $T$ be a finite (for every
$\omega$)  $\{\sFEd_t\}_{t\geq 0}$-stopping time,
let $\sG$ be a sub-$\sigma$-field of $\sFEd_T$,
and assume that $\P_1|{\sG}\ll\P_2|_{\sG}$.
Then there exists a unique measure, denoted
$\P_1\otimes_{T,\sG}\P_2$, such that
\bdes
\item[(a)]
$\P_1\otimes_{T,\sG}\P_2[A]=\P_1[A],
\quad A\in\sFEd_T,$
\item[(b)]
for every set $B\in\sG\vee\sigma(\Delta(X,T))$,
every version of $\P_2[B\,|\,\sG]$ is a
version of
$(\P_1\otimes_{T,\sG}\P_2)[B\,|\,\sFEd_T]$,
\item[(c)]
if $\P_1$ and $\P_2$ agree on  $\sG$, then
$\P_1\otimes_{T,\sG}\P_2$ and $\P_2$ agree on
$\sG\vee\sigma(\Delta(X,T))$.
\edes
\ecor

\noi
{\sc Proof:}
Because $\OmegaEd$ is a Polish space, there
\gbmarginpar{The first two paragraphs of this proof
  are modified (and slightly shorter).
exists a $\sG$-measurable probability kernel $Q$ from
$(\OmegaEd,\sFEd)$ to $(\OmegaEd,\sFEd)$ such that for every
$F\in\sFEd$, $Q(\cdot,F)$ is a version of $\P_2[F\,|\,\sG]$
(\cite{SV2}, Theorem 1.1.6).  Using Proposition \ref{P3.5}, we define
$\P_1\otimes_{T,\sG}\P_2\define\P_1\otimes_TQ$.  Property (a) of the
corollary is property (a) of Proposition \ref{P3.5}.

Given $\omega \in \OmegaEd$ and $F \in \sFEd$,
set $\Qhat(\omega, F) = (\delta_\omega
\otimes_{T(\omega)}Q(\omega,\cdot))[F]$.  Property (b) of Proposition
\ref{P3.5} asserts that $\Qhat(\cdot, F)$ is version of
$(\P\otimes_TQ)[F\,|\,\sFEd_T]$ for all $F \in \sFEd$.
Galmarino's Test (see \cite{DM}
Theorem~IV.100) remains valid for the filtered space $(\OmegaEd,\sFEd,
\{\sFEd_t\}_{t\geq 0})$, so $\Qhat(\omega, A \cap F) = \ind_A(\omega)
\Qhat(\omega, F)$ for all $\omega \in \OmegaEd$, $A \in \sFEd_T$, and
$F \in \sFEd$ by \eqref{eq:2}.  If $B$ takes the form
$B=A\cap\{\Delta(X,T)\in D\}$ with $A\in\sG$ and $D\in\frakC_0^d$,
then \eqref{eq:3} implies
\begin{equation}
  \label{eq:4}
  \Qhat(\cdot, B)
  = \ind_A Q(\cdot, \{\Delta(X, T) \in D\})
    = \P_2[B\,|\,\sG], \quad \P_2\mbox{-a.s.}
\end{equation}
It then follows from Dynkin's $\pi$-$\lambda$
theorem that \eqref{eq:4} holds for
all $B \in \sG\vee\sigma(\Delta(X,T))$.
From (a) we have
$\P_1\otimes_{T,\sG}\P_2|_{\sG}=\P_1|_{\sG}$,
and  we have assumed
$\P_1|_{\sG}\ll\P_2|_{\sG}$,
so the fact that $\Qhat(\cdot, B)$ is a version
of both $(\P_1\otimes_{T,\sG}\P_2)[B\,|\,\sFEd_T]$
and $\P_2[B\,|\,\sG]$
implies that every version of
$\P_2[B\,|\,\sG]$ is also a version of
$(\P_1\otimes_{T,\sG}\P_2)[B\,|\,\sFEd_T]$.

For (c), assume that $\P_1$ and $\P_2$ agree
\gbmarginpar{The remainder of the proof (and section) is unchanged.
on $\sG$.  Property (a) implies that
$\P_1|_{\sG}=(\P_1\otimes_{T,\sG}\P_2)|_{\sG}$,
and hence
$\P_2|_{\sG}=\P_1\otimes_{T,\sG}\P_2|_{\sG}$.
For $B\in\sG\vee\sigma(\Delta(X,T))$,
we have from (b) that
$\P_2[B\,|\,\sG]
=(\P_1\otimes_{T,\sG}\P_2)[B\,|\,\sG]$,
and we can integrate both sides over $\OmegaEd$
with respect to
$\P_2|_{\sG}=\P_1\otimes_{T,\sG}\P_2|_{\sG}$
to obtain (c).

Uniqueness of $\P_1\otimes_{T,\sG}\P_2$
follows from the fact that (b) specifies this
measure on $\sG\vee\sigma(\Delta(X,T))$
conditioned on $\sFEd_T$, up to
$\P_2|_{\sG}$-equivalence.  Furthermore, (a)
specifies this measure to be $\P_1$ on $\sFEd_T$,
and hence on $\sG$.
But $\P_1\ll\P_2$, and hence the integral
in the equation
$(\P_1\otimes_{T,\sG}\P_2)[B]
=\int_{\OmegaEd}\P_2[B\,|\,\sG]\,d\P_1$ for
$B\in\sG\vee\sigma(\Delta(X,T))$
is well defined.
We see then that properties (a) and (b)
specify the measure $\P_1\otimes_{T,\sG}\P_2$ on
$\sG\vee\sigma(\Delta(X,T))$
and on $\sFEd_T$.  These
two $\sigma$-fields generate $\sFEd$, and thus
the measure is uniquely determined
on $\sFEd$ by properties (a) and (b).
$\endproof$

\bp[Three-fold concatenation]\label{P3.7}
Let $\P_1$, $\P_2$ and $\P_3$ be probability
measures on $\OmegaEd$ and let $0\leq S\leq T$ be
finite (for every $\omega$)
$\{\sFEd_t\}_{t\geq 0}$-stopping times.  Let
$\sG$ be a sub-$\sigma$-field of $\sFEd_S$
and let $\sH$ be a sub-$\sigma$-field of
$\sG\vee\sigma(\Delta(X^T,S))$, which is a
sub-$\sigma$-field of $\sFEd_T$.  Assume that
$T-S$ is
$\sG\vee\sigma(\Delta(X,S))$-measurable.
If $\P_1|_{\sG}\ll\P_2|_{\sG}$ and
$\P_2|_{\sH}\ll\P_3|_{\sH}$, then
\bdes
\item[(a)]
$\P_1|_{\sG}\ll
(\P_2\otimes_{T,\sH}\P_3)|_{\sG}$,
\item[(b)]
$(\P_1\otimes_{S,\sG}\P_2)|_{\sH}
\ll\P_3|_{\sH}$,
\edes
so that both
$\P_1\otimes_{S,\sG}(\P_2\otimes_{T,\sH}\P_3)$
and
$(\P_1\otimes_{S,\sG}\P_2)\otimes_{T,\sH}\P_3$
are defined, and
\bdes
\item[(c)]
$\P_1\otimes_{S,\sG}(\P_2\otimes_{T,\sH}\P_3)
=(\P_1\otimes_{S,\sG}\P_2)\otimes_{T,\sH}\P_3$.
\edes
\ep

\noi
{\sc Proof:}
We simplify notation by writing
$\P_{12}=\P_1\otimes_{S,\sG}\P_2$,
$\P_{23}=\P_2\otimes_{T,\sH}\P_3$,
$\P_{1,23}=\P_1\otimes_{S,\sG}
(\P_2\otimes_{T,\sH}\P_3)$, and
$\P_{12,3}=(\P_1\otimes_{S,\sG}\P_2)
\otimes_{T,\sH}\P_3$.
For (a), we note from Corollary \ref{C3.6}(a)
that $\P_{23}$ agrees with $\P_2$ on $\sFEd_T$,
and hence on $\sG$.  Property (a) follows from
$\P_1|_{\sG}\ll\P_2|_{\sG}$.
For (b), let $A\in\sH$ satisfy $\P_3[A]=0$.  By
assumption, we also have $\P_2[A]=0$, and hence
$0$ is a version of $\P_2[A\,|\,\sG]$.  Being in
$\sH$, $A$ is also in
$\sG\vee\sigma(\Delta(X,S))$, and according to
Corollary \ref{C3.6}(b), $0$ is a version of
$\P_{12}[A\,|\,\sFEd_S]$.  Therefore, $\P_{12}[A]=0$.

The collection of sets of the form
$A\cap B\cap C$, where
$A\in\sFEd_S$, $B\in\sigma(\Delta(X^T,S))$,
and $C\in\sigma(\Delta(X,T))$, is closed under
finite intersections and generates $\sFEd$.
Thus, to prove (c), it suffices to show
that the desired equation holds when both sides
are evaluated for a set of this form.  Let $A$,
$B$ and $C$ be as described, and let $G$ be
in $\sG$.  Let $Z$ be a version of
$\E_3[\ind_C\,|\,\sH]$ and $Y$ a version of
$\E_2[\ind_BZ\,|\,\sG]$.  Corollary \ref{C3.6}(b)
implies that $Z$ is a version of
$\P_{23}[C\,|\,\sFEd_T]$.    This combined with
Corollary \ref{C3.6}(a) implies
$$
\E_{23}[\ind_GY]
=\E_2[\ind_GY]
=\E_2[\ind_{G\cap B}Z]
=\E_{23}[\ind_{G\cap B}Z]
=\E_{23}[G\cap B\cap C].
$$
We see then that
$Y=\E_2[\ind_B\E_3[\ind_C\,|\,\sH]\,|\,\sG]$
is a version of $\E_{23}[\ind_{B\cap C}\,|\,\sG]$,
a fact we use along with repeated applications
of Corollary \ref{C3.6}(a), (b) and (c) in the
chain of equalities
\beas
\P_{1,23}[A\cap B\cap C]
&=&
\E_{1,23}\Big[\ind_A\E_{1,23}[\ind_{B\cap C}\,|\,
\sFEd_S]\big]\\
&=&
\E_{1,23}
\big[\ind_A\E_{23}[\ind_{B\cap C}\,|\,\sG]\big]\\
&=&
\E_{1,23}\Big[\ind_A\E_2
\big[\ind_B\E_3[\ind_C\,|\,\sH]\,\big|\,\sG\big]\Big]\\
&=&
\E_1\Big[\ind_A\E_2
\big[\ind_B\E_3[\ind_C\,|\,\sH]\,\big|\,\sG\big]\Big]\\
&=&
\E_{12}\Big[\ind_A\E_{12}\big[\ind_B\E_3
[\ind_C\,|\,\sH]\,\big|\,\sFEd_S\big]\Big]
\\
&=&
\E_{12}\big[\ind_{A\cap B}
\E_3[\ind_C\,|\,\sH]\big]\\
&=&
\E_{12,3}\big[\ind_{A\cap B}\E_{12,3}
[\ind_C\,|\,\sFEd_S]\big]\\
&=&
\P_{12,3}[A\cap B\cap C].\hspace{1.8in}\endproof
\eeas

\noi
{\sc Proof of Theorem \ref{T3.3}:}
Let $m$ satisfy $0\leq m\leq n-1$.
According to Definition \ref{D3.2},
$$
\sG_{m+1}\subset\sH_{m+1}
=\sG_m\vee
\sigma\big(\Delta(X^{T_{m+1}},T_m)\big)
\subset\sG_m\vee
\sigma\big(\Delta(X,T_m)\big).
$$
If $0\leq m\leq n-2$, we further have
$$
\sG_{m+2}\subset\sH_{m+2}=\sG_{m+1}\vee
\sigma\big(\Delta(X^{T_{m+2}},T_{m+1})\big)
\subset\sG_m\vee\sigma\big(\Delta(X,T_m)\big).
$$
Iterating this process, we obtain the relation
$\sG_{j}\subset\sG_m\vee
\sigma\big(\Delta(X,T_m)\big)$ for
$j=m,m+1,\dots,n$.
Consequently,
\be\label{3.10}
\sG_j\vee
\sigma\big(\Delta(X^{T_{j+1}},T_j)\big)
\subset\sG_m\vee
\sigma\big(\Delta(X,T_m)\big),\quad
0\leq m\leq j\leq n.
\ee

We now proceed by induction on $m$.
The induction hypothesis corresponding to $m$,
where $m=0,\dots,n$, is
the existence of a measure $\P^m$ such that
\bdes
\item[(i)]
$\P^m[A]=\P[A]$ for all $A\in\sH_i$ and
$0\leq i\leq n+1$,
\item[(ii)]
for $B\in\sH_{i+1}$ and $0\leq i\leq m-1$,
every $\P$-version of $\P[B\,|\,\sG_i]$ is a
$\P^m$-version of  $\P^m[B\,|\,\sFEd_{T_i}]$.
\edes
The base case is $\P^0=\P$, a case for which (i)
trivially holds and (ii) is vacuous.

Assume the induction hypothesis for some
integer $m$.
Because $\sG_{m}\subset\sH_{m}$ and the measures
$\P^m$ and $\P$ agree on $\sH_{m}$, we may
invoke Corollary \ref{C3.6} to define
$\P^{m+1}\define\P^m\otimes_{T_{m},\sG_{m}}\P$.
If $A\in\sH_j$ for some $j$, $0\leq j\leq m$,
then $A\in\sFEd_{T_{m}}$ and
$\P^{m+1}[A]=\P^{m}[A]=\P[A]$ by Corollary
\ref{C3.6}(a) and part (i) of the induction
hypothesis.  If $m\leq j\leq n$,
then (\ref{3.10}) implies
\be\label{HinG}
\sH_{j+1}\define\sG_j\vee\sigma
\big(\Delta(X^{T_{j+1}},T_j)\big)
\subset\sG_{m}\vee
\sigma\big(\Delta(X,T_{m})\big).
\ee
But Corollary \ref{C3.6}(c) implies that
$\P^{m+1}$ agrees with $\P$ on
$\sG_m\vee\sigma\big(\Delta(X,T_m)\big)$.
Hence, $\P^{m+1}$ satisfies (i).

For some $i$, $0\leq i\leq m-1$, let
$B\in\sH_{i+1}$ and $A\in\sFEd_{T_i}$ be given.
Suppose $Z$ is a version of $\P[B\,|\,\sG_i]$, so
that both $A\cap B$ and $\ind_AZ$ are
$\sFEd_{T_m}$-measurable (recall
(\ref{3.1a})).  Corollary
\ref{C3.6}(a) (used twice)
and part (ii) of the induction
hypothesis imply
$$
\E^{m+1}[\ind_AZ]=\E^m[\ind_AZ]=\P^m[A\cap B]
=\P^{m+1}[A\cap B],
$$
showing that $Z$ is a version of
$\P^{m+1}[B\,|\,\sFEd_{T_i}]$.  Finally, suppose
$B$ is in $\sH_{m+1}$, which is a
sub-$\sigma$-field of
$\sG_m\vee\sigma(\Delta(X,T_m))$.
Corollary \ref{C3.6}(b) says that every version
of $\P[B\,|\,\sG_m]$ is a version of
$\P^{m+1}[B\,|\,\sFEd_{T_m}]$.  This establishes
(ii) with $m+1$ replacing $m$.

The induction argument above constructs
$\P^{\otimes\Pi}\define\P^{n+1}$ that satisfies
(\ref{3.2}) and (\ref{3.3}).  To see that this
measure is unique, we show that (\ref{3.2}) and
(\ref{3.3}) determine its value on sets of the
form $\cap_{i=0}^{n+1}B_i$, where
$B_0\in\sFEd_0=\sH_0$
and
$B_{i+1}\in\sigma(\Delta(X^{T_{i+1}},T_i))
\subset\sH_{i+1}$
for $i=0,\dots,n$.  This collection of sets
is closed under finite intersections and
generates $\sFEd$.  For such a set, repeated
application of (\ref{3.3}), followed
by a final application of (\ref{3.2}), yields
\gbmarginpar{I removed the break in the following
  display because it all fits on one page now.
\bea
\lefteqn{
\P^{\otimes\Pi}\big[\cap_{i=0}^{n+1}B_i\big]}
\nonumber\\
&=&
\E^{n+1}\Big[\ind_{B_0}\E^{n+1}
\big[\ind_{B_1}\cdots
\E^{n+1}\big[
\ind_{B_n}\E^{n+1}[\ind_{B_{n+1}}\,|\,\sFEd_{T_n}]
\,\big|\,\sFEd_{T_{n-1}}\big]
\cdots\,\big|\,\sFEd_0\big]\Big]
\nonumber\\
&=&
\E^{n+1}\Big[\ind_{B_0}\E^{n+1}
\big[\ind_{B_1}\cdots
\E^{n+1}\big[
\ind_{B_n}\E[\ind_{B_{n+1}}\,|\,\sG_n]
\,\big|\,\sFEd_{T_{n-1}}\big]
\cdots\,\big|\,\sFEd_0\big]\Big]
\nonumber\\
&=&
\E^{n+1}\Big[\ind_{B_0}\E^{n+1}
\big[\ind_{B_1}\cdots
\E\big[\ind_{B_n}\E[\ind_{B_{n+1}}\,|\,\sG_n]
\big]\sG_{n-1}\big]
\cdots\,\big|\,\sFEd_0\big]\Big]
\nonumber\\
&\vdots&\nonumber\\
&=&
\E^{n+1}\Big[\ind_{B_0}\E\big[\ind_{B_1}\cdots
\E\big[\ind_{B_n}\E[\ind_{B_{n+1}}\,|\,\sG_n]
\,\big|\,\sG_{n-1}\big]
\cdots\,\big|\,\sG_0\big]\Big]\nonumber\\
&=&
\E\Big[\ind_{B_0}\E\big[\ind_{B_1}\cdots
\E\big[\ind_{B_n}\E[\ind_{B_{n+1}}\,|\,\sG_n]
\,\big|\,\sG_{n-1}\big]
\cdots\,\big|\,\sG_0\big]\Big].\label{3.11}
\eea
This concludes the proof of Theorem
\ref{T3.3}.$\endproof$

\br\label{R3.8}
{\rm
We see from the proof of Theorem \ref{T3.3} that
$$
\P^{\otimes\Pi}
=\P\otimes_{T_0,\sG_0}\P\otimes_{T_1,\sG_1}
\cdots
\otimes_{T_n,\sG_n}\P,
$$
where the associative property of Proposition
\ref{P3.7}(c) makes the grouping of the
$\otimes_{T_i,\sG_i}$ operators irrelevant.
Equation (\ref{3.11}) provides insight into
the nature of  $\P^{\otimes\Pi}$.  If $\sG_i$
is equal to $\sFEd_{T_i}$ for each $i$, then the
last iterated conditional expectation in
(\ref{3.11}) collapses to
$\P[\cap_{i=0}^{n+1}B_i]$, and
$\P^{\otimes\Pi}$ agrees with $\P$.  At the
other extreme, if $\sG_i$ is the trivial
$\sigma$-field $\{\emptyset,\OmegaEd\}$ for each
$i$, then this iterated conditional expectation
becomes $\prod_{i=0}^{n+1}\P[B_i]$, and
increments of the path fragments over
$[T_i,T_{i+1}]$ are  independent of one another
under $P^{\otimes\Pi}$ but have the same unconditional
distribution as under $\P$.
$\endproof$
}
\er

\subsection{Properties preserved by
concatenation}\label{SPropPres}

\bp\label{P3.9}
Let $\P$ be a probability measure and let
$(T_i,\sG_i)_{i=0}^n$ be an extended
partition on
\gbmarginpar{Added $\{\sFEd_t\}_{t\geq 0}$-adapted
$(\OmegaEd,\sFEd)$.  Let $A$ be an $\{\sFEd_t\}_{t\geq 0}$-adapted continuous
real-valued process on $\OmegaEd$, and assume
that $\Delta(A,T_i)$ is
$\sG_i\vee\sigma(\Delta(X,T_i))$-measurable for
$i=0,\dots,n$.
\bdes
\item[(a)]
The total variation of $A$ on $[0,\infty)$
is $\P$-almost surely finite if and only if
it is $\P^{\otimes\Pi}$-almost surely finite.
\item[(b)]
The process $A$ is $\P$-almost surely absolutely
continuous if and only if it
is $\P^{\otimes\Pi}$-almost surely absolutely continuous.
\edes
\ep

\noi
{\sc Proof:}
We set $\P^0=\P$ and
$\P^{i+1}=\P^i\otimes_{T_i,\sG_i}\P$,
$i=1,\dots,n$.
Then $\P^{\otimes\Pi}=\P^{n+1}$.
For (a), we proceed by induction
on $i=0,1,\dots,n$, assuming that
\bdes
\item[(a$\mbox{}_i$)]
the total variation of $A$ on $[0,\infty)$
is $\P$-almost surely finite if and only if
it is $\P^i$-almost surely finite.
\edes
On $\sFEd_{T_i}$, the probability measures $\P^i$
and $\P^{i+1}$ agree (Corollary \ref{C3.6}(a)),
and hence $A$ restricted
to $[0,T_i]$ is $\P^i$-a.s.\ of finite
variation if and only if $A$ restricted to
$[0,T_i]$ is $\P^{i+1}$-a.s.\ of finite
variation.  The variation of $A$
on subintervals in $[T_i,\infty)$ is a function
of $\Delta(A,T_i)$, which is
$\sG_i\vee\sigma(\Delta(X,T_i))$-measurable,
and on this $\sigma$-field, the measures $\P^i$
and $\P^{i+1}$ agree (Corollary \ref{C3.6}(c)).
Therefore,   $A$ restricted to $[T_i,\infty)$
is $\P^i$-a.s.\ of finite variation if and only
if $A$ restricted to $[T_i,\infty)$ is
$\P^{i+1}$-a.s.\ of finite variation.  We
conclude that
$A$ has finite total variation on $[0,\infty)$
$\P^i$-almost surely if and only if it has
finite total variation $\P^{i+1}$-almost surely.
Combining this with the
induction hypothesis (a$\mbox{}_i$),  we obtain
the induction hypothesis with $i+1$ replacing
$i$.

The continuous process $A$ is absolutely
continuous on $[0,\infty)$ if and only if it is
absolutely continuous on $[0,T_i]$ and
absolutely continuous on $[T_i,\infty)$.
Therefore, we can imitate the proof of (a)
to obtain (b).  $\endproof$

\bp\label{P3.10}
Let $\P$ be a probability measure and let
$(T_i,\sG_i)_{i=0}^n$ be an extended
partition on
\gbmarginpar{Added $\{\sFEd_t\}_{t\geq 0}$-adapted
$(\OmegaEd,\sFEd)$.  Let $A$ be an
$\{\sFEd_t\}_{t\geq 0}$-adapted continuous
$\R^d$-valued process on $\OmegaEd$
with $A_0=0$,
and assume that $\Delta(A,T_i)$ is
$\sG_i\vee\sigma(\Delta(X,T_i))$-measurable for
$i=0,\dots,n$.
Assume there exists a measurable $\R^d$-valued
process $\alpha$ such that the set
\be\label{3.14}
J(\omega)\define\left\{t\in[0,\infty):
\frac{\partial}{\partial t}A_t(\omega)
\mbox{ exists but is not equal to }
\alpha_t(\omega)\right\}
\ee
has Lebesgue measure zero for
$\P$-almost every and $\Pc$-almost every
$\omega\in\OmegaEd$.  Then
\be\label{3.15}
\P\left[A_t=\int_0^t\alpha_udu
\,\,\forall t\in[0,\infty)\right]=1
\ee
if and only if
\be\label{3.16}
\P^{\otimes\Pi}\left[A_t=\int_0^t\alpha_udu
\,\,\forall t\in[0,\infty)\right]=1.
\ee
When the equalities (\ref{3.15}) and
(\ref{3.16}) hold, we also have
\be\label{3.17}
\E\int_0^{S}f(\alpha_u)\,du
=\E^{\otimes\Pi}\int_0^{S}
f(\alpha_u)\,du
\ee
for every nonnegative, Borel-measurable function
$f\colon\R^d\rightarrow\R$ and
$\{\sFEd_t\}_{t\geq 0}$-stopping
time $S$ satisfying
$(S-T_i)^+\in\sG_i\vee\sigma(\Delta(X,T_i))$
for $i=0,\dots,n$.
\ep

\noi
{\sc Proof:}
Assume (\ref{3.15}).
Then each component of $A$ is $\P$-a.s.\ absolutely continuous.
Proposition \ref{P3.9} implies that the components of $A$ are
$\P^{\otimes\Pi}$-a.s.\ absolutely continuous
as well.  Therefore, for
$\P^{\otimes\Pi}$-almost every $\omega$, the set
$$
C(\omega)\define\left\{t\in[0,\infty):
\frac{\partial}{\partial t}A_t(\omega)
\mbox{ exists}\right\}
$$
has full Lebesgue measure, and by the assumption
about $J(\omega)$, the set
$$
D(\omega)\define\left\{t\in[0,\infty):
\frac{\partial}{\partial t}A_t(\omega)
\mbox{ exists and is equal to }
\alpha_t(\omega)\right\}
$$
also has full Lebesgue measure for
$\P^{\otimes\Pi}$-almost
every $\omega$.  This implies (\ref{3.16}).
This argument is reversible; (\ref{3.16})
implies (\ref{3.15}).

We now assume (\ref{3.15}) and (\ref{3.16}).
The
$\sG_i\vee\sigma(\Delta(X,T_i))$-measurability
of $\Delta(A,T_i)$ together with
the $\sFEd_{T_{i+1}}$-measurability of
$\Delta(A^{T_{i+1}},T_i)$
implies the
$\sH_{i+1}$-measurability of
$\Delta(A^{T_{i+1}},T_i)$.
Because $A$ is adapted and continuous,
$A_{T_i(\omega)+t}(\omega)
\ind_{\{0\leq t< T_{i+1}(\omega)-T_i(\omega)\}}$
is a jointly
$\sH_{i+1}\otimes{\cal B}[0,\infty)$-measurable
function of $(\omega,t)$, where $\sB[0,\infty)$
is the Borel $\sigma$-field on $[0,\infty)$ (recall
Remark \ref{R3.2}).  The same is then true for
the right-hand derivative
$\frac{\partial^+}{\partial t}A_{T_i(\omega)+t}
\ind_{\{0\leq t< T_{i+1}(\omega)
-T_i(\omega)\}}$, where we set this
right-hand derivative equal to
an arbitrary value whenever
the limit of the relevant difference quotient
does not exist.
By assumption, $(S-T_i)^+$ is also
$\sG_i\vee\sigma(\Delta(X,T_i))$-measurable.
Therefore,
$(T_{i+1}-T_i)\wedge(S-T_i)^+
=T_{i+1}\wedge S-T_i\wedge S$
is $\sH_{i+1}$-measurable.
But on each $\sH_{i+1}$, the measures $\P$
and $\P^{\otimes\Pi}$ agree, which implies
that for every nonnegative Borel-measurable
function $f\colon\R^d\rightarrow\R$,
$$
\E\int_0^{T_{i+1}\wedge S-T_i\wedge S}
f(\alpha_{T_i+u})\,du
=\E^{\otimes\Pi}
\int_0^{T_{i+1}\wedge S-T_i\wedge S}
f(\alpha_{T_i+u})\,du.
$$
Summing over $i=0,1,\dots,n$,
we obtain (\ref{3.17}).
$\endproof$

\bex[Example \ref{SimpExPart1} continued]
{\rm
Consider the extended partition and
probability measures $\P$ and $\Pc$
of Example \ref{SimpExPart1}.
We take $A=X$ so that $A_0=0$ and
$\Delta(A,T_i)$ is
$\sG_1\vee\sigma(\Delta(X,T_i))$-measurable
for $i=0,1$.
We define the adapted processes
\begin{align*}
  \alpha_t(\omega)
  &= \Bigl\{\limsup_{\epsilon\downarrow 0}
          0 \vee \frac{\omega(\epsilon)}{\epsilon} \wedge 1\Bigr\}
          \; \ind_{(0,\infty]}(t),
  \\
  \beta_t(\omega)
  &= \Bigl\{\limsup_{\epsilon\downarrow 0}
          0 \vee \frac{\omega(\epsilon)}{\epsilon} \wedge 1\Bigr\}
          \; \ind_{(0,1]}(t)
    + \Bigl\{\limsup_{\epsilon\downarrow 0}
          0 \vee \frac{\omega(1+\epsilon)-\omega(1)}{\epsilon} \wedge 1\Bigr\}
          \; \ind_{(1,\infty]}(t),
\end{align*}
and the sets $E = \{A_t=\int_0^t\alpha_u \, du \, \;\forall
t\in[0,\infty)\}$ and $F = \{A_t=\int_0^t\beta_u \, du \, \;\forall
t\in[0,\infty)\}$.  Then
we have $\P[E] = \P[F] = \Pc[F] = 1$, but
$\Pc[E] = 1/2$.

If we let $K(\omega)$ denote the set obtained by replacing $\alpha$
with $\beta$ in \eqref{3.14}, then we see that $K(\omega)$ is a
Lebesgue null set $\P$-almost surely and $\P^{\otimes\Pi}$-almost
surely.  On the other hand,
$J(\omega)$ defined by \eqref{3.14}
is a Lebesgue null set $\P$-almost surely, but has
strictly positive Lebesgue measure with
strictly positive
$\P^{\otimes\Pi}$-probability.  In particular,
we see that
\eqref{3.15} and \eqref{3.16} may
not be equivalent in this situation.
$\endproof$ }
\eex



\bcor\label{C3.11}
Let $\P$ be a probability measure on
$(\OmegaEd,\sFEd)$ and for each positive integer
$m$, let
$\Pi^m\define(T_i^m,\sG_i^m)_{i=0}^{N(m)}$
be an extended partition.  Let $A$ be an
\gbmarginpar{Added $\{\sFEd_t\}_{t\geq 0}$-adapted and abbreviated
  almost surely to a.s.
$\{\sFEd_t\}_{t\geq 0}$-adapted
continuous $\R^d$-valued process on
$\OmegaEd$ with $A_0=0$, and assume that
$T^m_i$ and $\Delta(A,T_i^m)$ are
$\sG_i^m\vee\sigma(\Delta(X,T_i^m))$-measurable
for $i=1,\dots,N(m)$ and $m=1,2\dots$.
Let $\alpha$ be a measurable $\R^d$-valued
process such that
$A_t=\int_0^t\alpha_udu$ for
{\em every} $t\geq 0$, $\P$-almost surely,
and assume that the set $J(\omega)$
defined by (\ref{3.14}) has Lebesgue
measure zero for {\em every} $\omega\in\OmegaEd$.
Finally, assume
\be\label{3.18b}
\E\int_0^t\|\alpha_u\|\,du<\infty,
\quad t\geq 0.
\ee
Then the following hold.
\bdes
\item[(a)]
For every $t\in[0,\infty)$,
$\alpha$ restricted to $[0,t]$ is uniformly
integrable with respect to
the collection of product measures
$\{\P^{\otimes\Pi^m}\times
\lambda_{[0,t]}\}_{m=1}^{\infty}$,
where $\lambda_{[0,t]}$ denotes Lebesgue
measure on $[0,t]$.
\item[(b)]
The collection of measures
$\{\P^{\otimes\Pi^m}\circ
A^{-1}\}_{m=1}^{\infty}$
on $C_0^d$ is tight.
\edes
\ecor

\noi
{\sc Proof:}
For (a), fix
$t\in[0,\infty)$.  Given $\epsilon>0$,
(\ref{3.18b}) guarantees that there exists
$M_\epsilon>0$ so large that
$\E\int_0^t\|\alpha_u\|
\ind_{\{\|\alpha_u\|\geq M_{\epsilon}\}}\,du
\leq\epsilon$.
Applying Proposition \ref{P3.10}
with $f(x)=\|x\|\ind_{\{\|x\|\geq M_{\epsilon}\}}$
and $S=t$, we obtain
$\E^{\otimes\Pi^m}
\int_0^t\|\alpha_u\|\ind_{\{\|\alpha_u\|\geq
M_{\epsilon}\}}\,du
\leq\epsilon$
for all $m$.

For (b) it
suffices to verify that for every
$\epsilon>0$, there exists a set
$\Omega_{\epsilon}\in\sFEd$ such that
$\P^{\otimes\Pi^m}(\Omega_{\epsilon})\geq
1-\epsilon$  for every $m$ and
\be\label{3.19b}
\lim_{\delta\downarrow 0}
\sup_{\omega\in \Omega_{\epsilon}}
\sup_{0\leq s\leq v\leq t\wedge (s+\delta)}
\|A_v(\omega)-A_s(\omega)\|=0,\quad t\geq 0.
\ee
Fix $\epsilon>0$ and let $\{t_n\}_{n=1}^{\infty}$ be an
increasing sequence of positive numbers with
$\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}t_n=\infty$.
For fixed $n$, we construct $\Omega_n$ such that
$\Pcm(\Omega_n)\geq 1-2^{-n}\epsilon$ for every $m$ and
\be\label{3.20b}
\lim_{\delta\downarrow 0}\sup_{\omega\in\Omega_n}
\sup_{0\leq s\leq v\leq t_n\wedge(s+\delta)}
\|A_v(\omega)-A_s(\omega)\|=0.
\ee
Then $\Omega_{\epsilon}=\cap_{n=1}^{\infty}\Omega_n$
satisfies (\ref{3.19b}) and $\Pcm(\Omega_{\epsilon})\geq 1-\epsilon$
for every $m$.

We fix $n$ and construct $\Omega_n$ by working through the proof
of the Borel-Cantelli lemma.
For each positive integer $k$,
part (a) implies the existence of $\delta_k>0$
for which
$$
\E^{\otimes\Pi^m}\left[
\sup_{0\leq s\leq v\leq t_n\wedge(s+\delta_k)}
\|A_v-A_s\|\right]\leq
\E^{\otimes\Pi^m}
\left[\sup_{0\leq s\leq v\leq t_n\wedge(s+\delta_k)}
\int_s^v\|\alpha_u\|\,du\right]
\leq
2^{-2k}
$$
for all $m$.
We define
$F_k=
\left\{\sup_{0\leq s\leq v\leq t_n\wedge(s+\delta_k)}
\int_s^v\|\alpha_u\|\,du\geq 2^{-k}\right\}$,
and note from Chebyshev's inequality
that $\Pcm(F_k)\leq 2^{-k}$ for every $m$ and $k$.
Choose $j$ such that $2^{-(j-1)}\leq 2^{-n}\epsilon$ and
set $\Omega_n=\cap_{k\geq j}F_k^c$.  We have
$\Pcm(\Omega_n^c)\leq \sum_{k=j}^{\infty}\Pcm(F_k)
\leq 2^{-n}\epsilon$ for every $m$, as desired.
Also, $\omega\in\Omega_n$ implies that
$\sup_{0\leq s\leq v\leq t_n\wedge(s+\delta_k)}
\int_s^v\|\alpha_u\|\,du\leq 2^{-k}$
for all $k\geq j$, and hence (\ref{3.20b}) holds.
$\endproof$

\begin{definition}\label{D3.11}
Let $Y$ be an adapted continuous $\R^d$-valued process
defined on a filtered probability
\gbmarginpar{Moved filtration to third slot in tuple.
space $(\Omega,\sF,\{\sF_t\}_{t\geq 0},\P)$, let $B$
be an adapted continuous $\R^d$-valued process whose components
are of finite variation and for which $B_0=0$, and let
$C$ be an adapted continuous,
$d\times d$-matrix-valued process whose components
are of finite variation and for which $C_0=0$.
We further assume that outside a $\P$-null set
that does not depend on $s$ and $t$,
the increment $C_t-C_s$ is positive semi-definite whenever
$0\leq s<t<\infty$.
We say that {\em $Y$ is a semimartingale
with characteristic pair $(B,C)$} if the components of
$Y-B$ and $(Y-B)(Y-B)^{tr}-C$ are local martingales.
\end{definition}

\bp\label{P3.12}
Let $\P$ be a probability measure and let
$(T_i,\sG_i)_{i=0}^n$ be an extended partition
on $(\OmegaEd,\sFEd)$.
Let $Y$ be a continuous $\R^{d'}$-valued process ($d'$ may
be different from $d$),
and suppose that $Y$ is a semimartingale with
characteristic pair
$(B,C)$ under $\P$.  If $\Delta(Y,T_i)$, $\Delta(B,T_i)$
and $\Delta(C,T_i)$ are all $\sG_i\vee\sigma(\Delta(X,T_i))$-measurable
for $i=1,\dots,n$, then under $\P^{\otimes\Pi}$ the process
$Y$ is still a semimartingale with characteristic pair
$(B,C)$.
\ep

The proof of Proposition \ref{P3.12} depends on
\gbmarginpar{A lemma has been removed.}
some preliminary results.

\bl\label{L3.14}
Let $\P_1$ and $\P_2$ be probability measures on
$(\OmegaEd,\sFEd)$, and let $T$ be a finite (for every $\omega$)
$\{\sFEd_t\}_{t\geq 0}$-stopping time.
Let $M$ be a continuous
local martingale relative to $\{\sFEd_t\}_{t\geq 0}$
under $\P_1$ and $\P_2$.
Let $\sG$ be a sub-$\sigma$-field of $\sFEd_T$ such that
$\P_1|_{\sG}\ll\P_2|_{\sG}$ and assume that
$\Mhat\define\Delta(M,T)$ is
$\sG\vee\sigma(\Delta(X,T))$-measurable.
Then $(M_t,\sFEd_t)_{t\geq 0}$
is a continuous local martingale under
$\P_{12}\define\P_1\otimes_{T,\sG}\P_2$.
\el

\noi
{\sc Proof:}
\gbmarginpar{This proof has changed.  There used to be
  another lemma before this proposition, but it has been removed and
  moved into this proof.  This saves almost a page and is easier to
  read.
It is sufficient to show that $M^T$ and $M - M^T$ are both
$\P_{12}$-local martingales relative to $\{\sFEd_t\}_{t\geq 0}$.  As
$M^T$ is a $\P_1$-local martingale, $M^T$ is $\sFEd_T$-measurable, and
$\P_1$ and $\P_{12}$ agree on $\sFEd_T$, we may immediately conclude
that $M^T$ is a $\P_{12}$-local martingale.

For each integers $n > 0$, define the stopping time
$S^n\define\inf\{t\geq T:|M_t-M_T|\geq n\}$.  Then $M^{S_n} -
(M^{S_n})^T = M^{S_n} - M^T$ is bounded, and $\Delta(M^{S_n}, T)$ is
$\sG\vee\sigma(\Delta(X,T))$-measurable.  As a result, we may assume
without loss of generality that $M - M^T$ is a uniformly integrable
$\P_{2}$-martingale.

We now show that $\Mhat$ is a $\P_{12}$-martingale with respect to
the filtration $\sFhat_t = \sF_{T+t}$.  The process $\Mhat$ is clearly
$\{\sFhat_t\}_{t\geq 0}$-adapted, and it follows from the optional
sampling theorem that $\Mhat$ is a $\P_2$-martingale with respect to
the filtration $\{\sFhat_t\}_{t\geq 0}$.  For $0\leq s\leq t$,
$A\in\sFEd_T$, and $B\in\sigma(\Delta_r(X,T) : 0 \leq r \leq s)$, we
have from Corollary \ref{C3.6}(b) that \beas \E_{12}\big[\ind_{A\cap
  B}\big(\Mhat_t -\Mhat_s\big)\big] &=& \E_{12}\Big[\ind_A\E_{12}
\big[\ind_B\big(\Mhat_t
-\Mhat_s\big)\,\big|\,\sFEd_T\big]\Big]\\
&=& \E_{12}\Big[\ind_A \E_2\big[\ind_B\big(\Mhat_t
-\Mhat_s\big)\,\big|\,\sG\big]\Big]\\
&=& \E_{12}\left[\ind_A\E_2\Big[\ind_B \E_2\big[\Mhat_t
  -\Mhat_s\,\big|\,\sFhat_s\big]\,\Big|\,\sG\Big]\right] \,\,=\,\, 0,
\eeas where we have used the fact that $\Mhat$ is $\P_2$-martingale in
the last step.  Writing $X^{T+s}_t = X^T_t + \Delta_{0\vee (t-T)
  \wedge s}(X, T)$, we see that sets of the form $A\cap B$ generate
$\sFhat_s$.  It then follows from Dynkin's $\pi$-$\lambda$ theorem
that $\Mhat$ is $\P_{12}$-martingale relative to $\{\sFhat_t\}_{t\geq
  0}$.

To conclude the proof, we observe that
\gbmarginpar{$\sF_{r \vee T} \subset \sFhat_{(r-T)\vee
    0} \subset \sF_{(r \vee T)+}$, but it is not clear to me that $\sF_{r
    \vee T} = \sFhat_{(r-T)\vee 0}$ without right-continuity, so
  I don't even mention $\sFhat_{(r-T)\vee 0}$.
$(r - T)^+$ is a bounded $\{\sFhat_t\}_{t\geq 0}$-stopping time and
$\sF_r \subset \sFhat_{(r-T)\vee 0}$ for each $r \geq 0$.  Fixing $0
\leq s < t$ and $A \in \sF_s$, we have
\begin{equation*}
  \E_{12}[\ind_A (M_t - M^T_t) ]
  = \E_{12}[\ind_A \Mhat_{(t-T)\vee 0}]
  = \E_{12}[\ind_A \Mhat_{(s-T)\vee 0}]
  = \E_{12}[\ind_A (M_s - M^T_s)],
\end{equation*}
so $M - M^T$ is $\P_{12}$-martingale relative to
$\{\sF_t\}_{t\geq 0}$.$\endproof$

\bl\label{L3.15}
Let $\P$ be a probability measure on $(\OmegaEd,\sFEd)$,
and let $M$ be a uniformly integrable $\P$-martingale
relative to $\{\sFEd_t\}_{t\geq 0}$.  Let $S$, $T$ and $U$
be stopping times with $T\leq U$ almost surely, and let
$Z$ be an $\sFEd_T$-measurable bounded random variable.  Then
$\E\big[(M_U-M_T)Z\,\big|\,\sFEd_S\big]
=(M_{U\wedge S}-M_{T\wedge S})Z$.
\el

\noi
{\sc Proof:}
Because
$$
\ind_{\{S\leq T\}}\E\big[(M_U-M_T)Z\,\big|\,\sFEd_S\big]
=\ind_{\{S\leq T\}}\E\Big[Z\E\big[(M_U-M_T)\,\big|\,\sFEd_T\big]
\,\Big|\,\sFEd_S\Big]
=0,
$$
we have
\beas
\hspace{0.75in}
\lefteqn{\E\big[(M_U-M_T)Z\,\big|\,\sFEd_S\big]}\\
&=&
\ind_{\{T<S\leq U\}}\E\big[(M_U-M_T)Z\,\big|\,\sFEd_S\big]
+\ind_{\{U<S\}}\E\big[(M_U-M_T)Z\,\big|\,\sFEd_S\big]\\
&=&
\ind_{\{T<S\leq U\}}(M_S-M_T)Z
+\ind_{\{U<S\}}(M_U-M_T)Z\\
&=&
(M_{U\wedge S}-M_{T\wedge S})Z.
\hspace{3.15in}\endproof
\eeas

\bl\label{L3.16}
Let $\P_1$ and $\P_2$
be probability measures on $(\OmegaEd,\sFEd)$
and let $T$ be a finite (for every $\omega$)
\gbmarginpar{Added hypen before stopping time and
  $\{\sFEd_t\}_{t\geq 0}$- before adapted.
$\{\sFEd_t\}_{t\geq 0}$-stopping time.
Let $M^1$, $M^2$ and $C$ be continuous
$\{\sFEd_t\}_{t\geq 0}$-adapted real-valued processes
such that $M^1$, $M^2$ and $M^3\define M^1M^2-C$ are local
martingales relative to $\{\sFEd_t\}_{t\geq 0}$ under $\P_1$ and $\P_2$.
Let $\sG$ be a sub-$\sigma$-field of $\sFEd_T$ such that
$\P_1|_{\sG}\ll\P_2|_{\sG}$ and assume that
$\Mhat^1\define\Delta(M^1,T)$,
$\Mhat^2\define\Delta(M^2,T)$ and $\Chat\define\Delta(C,T)$
are $\sG\vee\sigma(\Delta(X,T))$-measurable.
Then $(M^3,\sFEd_t)_{t\geq 0}$ is a
local martingale under $\P_{12}\define\P_1\otimes_{\sG,T}\P_2$.
\el

\noi
{\sc Proof:}
We cannot apply Lemma \ref{L3.14} directly because we
did not assume that
$\Mhat_3$ is $\sG\vee\sigma(\Delta(X,T))$-measurable.
Instead, we define the process
\beas
Y_t
&\define&
M_{t\wedge T}^1M_{t\wedge T}^2
+(M_t^1-M_{t\wedge T}^1)(M_t^2-M_{t\wedge T}^2)-C_t\\
&=&
M_t^3-(M_t^1-M_{t\wedge T}^1)M_{t\wedge T}^2
-(M_t^2-M_{t\wedge T}^2)M_{t\wedge T}^1,\quad t\geq 0,
\eeas
for which $\Delta(Y,T)=\Delta(M^1,T)\Delta(M^2,T)-\Delta(C,T)$ is
$\sG\vee\sigma(\Delta(X,T))$-measurable.
Define
$T_n\define
\inf\big\{t\geq 0:|M_t^1|\vee|M_t^2|\vee|M_t^3|
\vee|C_t|\geq n\big\}$,
and set $M^{i,n}\define (M^i)^{T_n}$ for $i=1,2,3$,
$C^n\define C^{T_n}$ and $Y^n\define Y^{T_n}$.  For fixed $n$,
the processes $M^{i,n}$, $i=1,2,3$, and $Y^n$ are bounded.
For $0\leq s\leq t$,
we apply Lemma \ref{L3.15} with $M=M^{1,n}$, $Z=M_{t\wedge T}^{2,n}$,
$S=s$, $T=t\wedge T$ and $U=t$, and use the fact that
$M_s^{1,n}-M_{s\wedge T}^{1,n}=0$ if $T\geq s$ to obtain
\bea
\E_k\big[(M_t^{1,n}-M_{t\wedge T}^{1,n})M_{t\wedge T}^{2,n}
\,\big|\,\sFEd_s\big]
&=&
(M_s^{1,n}-M_{s\wedge T}^{1,n})M_{t\wedge T}^{2,n}\nonumber\\
&=&
(M_s^{1,n}-M_{s\wedge T}^{1,n})M_{s\wedge T}^{2,n},
\quad k=1,2.\quad\quad\label{3.24}
\eea
The same equality holds if we reverse the roles of $M^{1,n}$
and $M^{2,n}$.  Finally, because $M^{3,n}$ is a martingale,
\beas
\E_k[Y_t^n\,|\,\sFEd_s]
&=&
\E_k[M_t^{3,n}\,|\,\sFEd_s]
-\E_k\big[(M_t^{1,n}-M_{t\wedge T}^{1,n})M_{t\wedge T}^{2,n}
\,\big|\,\sFEd_s\big]\\
&&\qquad
-\E_k\big[(M_t^{2,n}-M_{t\wedge T}^{2,n}\big)M_{t\wedge T}^{1,n}
\,\big|\,\sFEd_s\big]\\
&=&
M_s^{3,n}-(M_s^{1,n}-M_{s\wedge T}^{1,n})M_{s\wedge T}^{2,n}
-(M_s^{2,n}-M_{s\wedge T}^{2,n})M_{s\wedge T}^{1,n}\\
&=&
Y_s^n,\quad k=1,2,
\eeas
so $Y$ is a local martingale under both $\P_1$ and $\P_2$.
Lemma \ref{L3.14} implies that $M^1$, $M^2$ and $Y$
are $\P_{12}$-local martingales.  Therefore, (\ref{3.24})
holds under $\P_{12}$ as well,
from which we conclude that
\beas
\hspace{0.4in}\E_{12}[M_t^{3,n}\,|\,\sFEd_s]
&=&
~~~
